Title: Speech at 2007 Business Forum in Kopaonik
text: 09/03/2007 Speech of Governor Jela.i. at d22007 Business Forumd3 in Kopaonik - After six years of transition during which two governments were in office, the time has come fora decision to be made on the future course of the transition process, said NBS Governor RadovanJela.i. at the d22007 Business Forum,d3 a meeting of economists currently taking place inKopaonik. In anticipation of the new government elect, Governor Jela.i. invited economic teamsof all major political parties to present their position on key economic issues that will shape thecountryd5s future economic policy. - The coming few weeks will be of key significance for the economic policy to be implemented bythe future government. Its course will depend on the response to a very exact question: will thebasic premises of the current economic policy be reviewed, including interaction of fiscal andmonetary policies in maintaining macroeconomic stability, or the new government will carry onfrom where the previous one will have left off, Jela.i. said. The Governor then singled out a number of issues on which the future government elect shouldformulate clear strategy from day one. - In terms of tax system, for instance, we need to choose between direct or indirect taxation. Inaddition, the government should make a decision on whether to increase its role in the pensionsystem and if so to what extent. But it also needs to decide whether to support the first pillar, i.e.state pensions, or to sway towards supporting the system of private pension funds throughadequate tax breaks. It is up to the new government to decide in very precise and time defined terms what it aims toachieve with respect to transformation of state and social ownership, especially in case of largepublic enterprises. Privatization of these enterprises still represents a great unknown, as there isno clear position as to what the government wishes to retain in its ownership and what it reallyintends to sell. This creates uncertainty not only in Serbia, but among potential foreign investorsas well because the message sent across is that d2everything and anything is possibled3. Such stateof affairs may weaken our d2line of defenced3 in future negotiations with international financialorganizations (IMF and World Bank, for instance), the support of which is instrumental in thecontinuation of the transition process in Serbia, Governor Jela.i. said. The new government, continued Governor Jela.i., should not only specify its plans regarding itsfuture role in the financial sector, as it holds majority stake in banks and insurance companies,but it should also announce how it proposes to finance large infrastructure projects such asCorridor 10 and to accomplish its declared objectives d0 further development of small andmedium-sized enterprises, development of underdeveloped regions, housing construction, etc.without disturbing the functioning of market mechanisms to any significant extent. Press Release from the Governord5s Office

PDF: Speech by Governor Radovan Jelasic on the 4th Sectoral Meeting on Economic and Financial Matters.pdf
Title: Speech on the 4th Sectoral Meeting on Economic and Financial Matters
text: 15/06/2007 Speech by Governor Radovan Jelasic on the 4th Sectoral Meeting onEconomic and Financial Matters EU d0 Republic of Serbia Enhanced Permanent Dialogue 4th Sectoral Meeting on Economic and Financial Matters Belgrade,ca June 14th - 15th, 2007 Ladies and gentlemen, dear friends, I am delighted to welcome you to Belgrade on behalf of the National Bank of Serbia as yourpresence here provides us with an additional strong ally on our challenging job to secure pricestability. This job is neither easy nor cheap.ca Despite hyperinflation that lasted for the longesttime ever in our modern times d0 25 monthsd0 we seem to be forgetting rather quickly and gettingused rather easily to the good results we are getting today!ca So quickly, that the media todayshow almost no interest in the recent inflation figures as it has moved back again to somed2normald3 levels.ca But, we should not take things for granted, at least not so fast, as the volume ofeffort involved in maintaining current results is way too substantial. Although, unfortunately, neither you nor the IMF have visited us since the beginning of this year,we used this time to deliver on our promises, just as if you were here!ca We might have even donea bit more, just to be on the safe side!ca I would like on this occasion to mention two key issuesthat are the topic of the presentation today as my colleagues will go into more details: 1. Monetary Policy Serbia de facto moved to the inflation targeting regime in September 2006 although de jureca westill need to adjust not only the official decision of the Government that still talks about thed2managed floatd3 exchange rate to d2free floatd3 regime but some of our internal rules andregulations as well.ca Despite that, the most challenging part of the job has already been donewith very concrete results: low inflation. Most of the people in Serbia do not remember suchca low level of inflation, 4.4% CPI and 3.0.%core inflation, from a very simple reason, as it took place last time some 44 years ago, namely in1963, and the majority of us were not born yet or were not interested in such issues at all.caDespite all the criticism and thanks to the hard work we achieved our goal last year d0 weremained firm on the road of inflation targeting and used interest rate as the main policy tool.caMonetary policy works in Serbia as well as inany other country in the region, and wider!ca Was iteasy d0 the answer is no. Was it cheap d0 the answer is again no.ca Was it necessary d0 the answer isabsolutely yes. During last 44 years, we got used to inflation to such an extent that no inflation is simplyunusual, even strange.ca It is like loosing part of your own history, a custom that wasaccompanying us for almost half of the last century.ca d2Buy today because tomorrow itca is going tobe more expensive!d3 - was the motto of living that we have to change and changes had to becarried out. If one looks forward and assuming at least a balanced budget, we expect the core inflation tocontinue to drop during the third quarter on a yearly level but that it will pick up in the lastquarter of this year.ca On the other hand, CPI inflation will start to rise as soon as in this month,not only because the inflation was zero in June and negative, 0.1% in July last year, but alsobecause of the increase of oil prices and the secondary effects of the electricity price increase ofsome 15% last month. Despite that, we are confident, that core inflation will be within our targetrange of 4 d0 8% with a chance of even undershooting it by the end of December this year.ca For2008 we target core inflation rate of 3 d0 6%! I do not want to waste your time by explaining the importance of price stability to growth,employment, equality within the society etc. as my colleagues from the ECB are much better inthat. But I do not want to raise the importance of a restrictive budget till the end of 2007especially regarding the wage bill and public consumption. NBS already has a proven track record regarding fighting inflation d0 namely, we successfullyneutralized increased public expenditures before the recent parliamentary elections in Januarythis year.ca It was a hard and very costly exercise but a successful one judged by the level ofinflation today.ca Although we won the battle the war is not over, yet.ca I honestly hope that thegovernment will participate on our side in the d2war against inflationd3 not only by talking but bycutting salaries and public expenditures as well.ca We simply cannot and should not continueincreasing all major categories of the budged by some 20-25% and expect a CPI rate of inflationof only 6-7%.ca The numbers simply do not add up except if the National bankcaca increases furtherthe level of monetary policy restrictiveness.ca Such an outcome is simply bad for all theparticipants, bad for the economy as it will result in lower growth, bad for the public d0 higher costof borrowing and last but not least, also bad for the income statement of the National Bank as itcases substantial additional costs. But the Law on the National Bank of Serbia is very clear - d2the primary objective of the NBS shallbe achieving and maintaining price stabilityd3.ca In view of the level ofca transition in Serbia today, wedid d2achieved3 high degree of price stability and we will use all the available tools and means ofthe central bank to d2maintaind3 it. ca 2. Exchange rate policy Our Dinar was never ever floating more freely than today and the level of transparency in the waythe exchange rate is set on a daily basis is exemplary. Serbia has been moving step by step duringlast 12 months to an absolutely free float. Since March this year, when we changed themethodology of calculating the medium exchange rate d0 instead of setting the rate a the fixingsession we now calculate it as a weighted average of all transactions that are taking place duringforeign exchange trading d0 the NBS was active only twice to quell extreme demand for foreignexchange caused by political uncertainties. Starting June 4th, we even abolished the mandatorydaily fixing organized by the National Bank. Despite all of these steps, the foreign currency reserves are at their record high level of USD12.3bn.ca Last year, in order to stop additional appreciation of the Dinar, we even bought over USD1.5bn from banks and the exchange bureaus.ca The best proof to what extent our currency isfloating freely is the depths of the foreign exchange market:ca the turnover between the banks inMay 2007 was as high as the total turnover in the year of 2005!. We plan to continue liberalization of the foreign exchange market by transferring the businesswith the exchange bureaus from the central bank to commercial banks in due course as well as bystronger involvement ofca foreign players on the foreign exchange market. Governord5s Office

PDF: Speech by Governor Radovan Jelasic on the occasion of the Conference on the Italian credit line for Balkan SMEs - Serbia.pdf
Title: Speech on the occasion of the Conference on the Italian credit line for Balkan SMEs - Serbia
text: 17/06/2007 Speech by Governor Radovan Jelasic on the occasion of the Conference on the Italian credit line for Balkan SMEs -Serbia Ladies and Gentlemen, I would like to welcome you all on the occasion of the conference on the Italian Credit line for the Balkan SMEs d0 Serbia. When somebody talks about SMEs financing in Serbia today, the National Bank of Serbia has to be mentioned for both direct and indirect reasons. Let me first start with the indirect reason. The role of the National Bank of Serbia has been clearly defined by the central bank law: d2The primary objective of the NBS shall be achieving and maintaining price stabilityd3. The reasoning behind this formulation is very simple. The experience of the last 2 to3 decades not only world-wide but in Serbia as well proves that nothing contributes more to higher growth, better standard of living, lower unemployment than price stability. To what extent has the National Bank of Serbia delivered on its d2primary objectived3? Well, numbers speak better than thousand words d0 the rate of inflation in Serbia / Yugoslavia today has not been seen since 1963. Moreover, inflationary expectations are at a low level as well, namely around 6 -7 % for this year compared to our core inflation target of some 4-8% set in August 2006 d0 our so called d2credibility gapd3 is down to only 1-2%! As a governor of the central bank, one always walks a fine line between criticizing the level of public expenditures and, at the same time, keeping inflationary expectations low. It is especially difficult when we have no anchors such as a binding program with the European Union or International Monetary Fund. Let me assure you that we will continue to undertake all necessary measures in order to keep inflation as low as it is d0 in line with our mandate d0 the key criteria to our success. It will be neither easy nor cheap, but is absolutely necessary for Serbia and its citizens. Price stability is especially important for SMEs as they have no access to insider information, politicians are not interested in them, and the government is not going to bail them out. In case of financial troubles most banks prefer to simply walk away from the SMEs ,so the little financing they get from commercial banks has to be replaced by the key financing source, which is friends and family! As far as direct involvement of the central bank in SMEs financing is concerned, probably no other central bank in the region has a more active role in that respect than the National Bank of Serbia. As agent for 3 credit lines, European Agency of Reconstruction, European Investment Bank and Italian government loan we have gained some valuable experience in SMEs financing in Serbia. I

PDF: Speech by Governor Jelasic at the Conference of the Centre for Democracy Economic and Social Rights in Serbia.pdf
Title: Speech at the Conference of the Centre for Democracy Economic and Social Rights in Serbia
text: 27/06/2008 Speech by Governor Jelasic at the Conference of the Centre forDemocracy d2Economic and Social Rights in Serbiad3 Ladies and Gentlemen, Allow me to extend my welcome to you all on behalf of the National Bank of Serbia. It is anhonour and a great pleasure for me to be invited to speak not only about inflation, interest rates,or even passports, but also about corporate social responsibility (CSR). By default, transition implies privatization, i.e. ownership transformation which is not an end initself but represents means for achieving a more efficient economy, stronger economic growthand, last but not least, the promise of a d2better lifed3. Ownership transformation has severalconflicting aims: allow me to point out one such major aim and to discuss the ensuing dilemmasd0 should the privatization revenue be the main criteria (everybody is happy to acquire a monopolyposition, and the foreigners are no exception) or should the state attach more importance towhat the new owner does with the privatized company, which brand product it produces, whathis attitude is towards the employees, etc. If price is not the only criterion, then the processgrows more complex and, we all agree, more efficient for the state. The NBS also lends a hand inthe process of ownership transformation. It approves privatization deals for banks and insurancecompanies, but not with the aim of enabling certain individuals to earn big money or replacingdomestic owner by a foreign one. Instead, it focuses on considering whether the new ownercontributes to the strengthening or to the weakening of the overall financial sector. In terms ofwork environment, professional prospects at home and abroad, wages and employersd5 attitude,bankers have an edge over others today and are a source of much envy. The above opening remarks serve to invite foreign investors to Serbia to join me and those whoshare my views. Unfortunately, eight years into the transition, we are still a minority and, I fear,we shall remain so for quite some time even if the change continues at the current pace.Foreigners are expected not only to invest in Serbia but also to refuse to accept d2balkanizationd3i.e. local peculiarities without considering their logic or necessity. Good business practices thatwe have to adopt also imply activities relating to corporate social responsibility. We rightfullyexpect the best practices to be applied in Serbia as well, and I see no reason for a delay in theirapplication. So far, foreign investors and foreign private institutions have shown greater social responsibilitythan the domestic companies, either socially or state-owned.ca The concept of corporate socialresponsibility is gaining popularity in Serbia and many companies and institutions, including theNBS, are its great advocates. Corporate social responsibility does not hurt, it is not expensive, buttakes time. Hence, we should stop from time to time to think what it really means. Besides numerous activities and initiatives which companies may participate in or undertake, it isimportant that they recognize the importance of social responsibility within their organizationalstructure d0 and to start from their own backyard. Naturally, we have a long way to go to attain USstandards in this respect. Namely, in the US they even organize annual competitions to choosed2100 best employersd3 where ranking is made exclusively in terms of the quality ofca employmentprogrammes and employee benefits. What the NBS has done so far and what makes us particularly proud are the benefits we provideto our employees, like the use of vacation homes and recreation facilities (instead of the earlierpractice of supplying fresh meat or granting d2May 1std3 prizes): 1.caRegionalization of business activities is not just an empty phrase, but a reality in the NationalBank. A) Solvency Department is located in Novi Sad and has 30 full time employed and around300 occasionally engaged in the receipt and processing of periodical financial reports, b) EnforcedCollection Department is located in Kragujevac and employs 48 persons, c) Call Centre is locatedin Uziceca and will, by the end of this year, have a staff of five, d) steps have been taken to organizethe central archives in Nis which will employ another 8 persons. This is challenging from the pointof view of human resources, work technology, logistical support, etc. but at the same time provesthat the NBS is not only Belgrade, but Serbia as well. If we could achieve such regionalization,than the same can be done by everybody else provided they are willing to do it. I am inviting themall to join us. We shall be glad to share our experiences. 2.caProfessional training plays the key role in the NBS. In addition to sending our staff to seminars,post-graduate and specialist courses at home and abroad, as well as foreign language courses, astudy on the career path of each and every employee will shortly be completed. Soon the oldprinciple of being a lifer in one department will become a thing of the past. Professional trainingis an employeed5s right, not a reward! 3.ca NBS organizes regular medical check-ups for its employees. There is a surgery in our officebuilding on Slavija where NBS staff can have all kinds of medical check-ups, from dental togynaecological. In addition, each year about one hundred employees are offered a possibility ofwhole stress testing. 4.caFrom the next year, disabled persons will have an equal employment opportunity in the NBS. Incooperation with the Centre for Development of Inclusive Society, the NBS will make all necessaryfacilities first in our Slavija office building and later in Kralja Petra Street.cacaca 5.caThe obligation to organize summer school for students was first imposed by the governor butsoon became a very popular programme well accepted by the NBS management staff.ca We shouldalso note our participation in the Career days across Serbia which aims to attract the beststudents both for internship and apprenticeship in the NBS.caca 6.caOur activities relating to waste paper recycling were not simple either but proved a success.Those who engage in recycling in the office tend to do the same at home as well. Some, includingmyself, bring their waste paper from home to recycle it in the office. Having to place additionalwaste paper baskets, organize tenders for waste paper disposal, give additional instructions tocleaning ladies, all of these were reasons against waste paper recycling and arguments that suchthings cannot be organized in Serbia and that we should best give up the idea. We have, however,persevered and achieved great success. 7.caPromotional activities relating to financial services consist of printing 23 different leaflets ofwhich 14 were printed in almost 2 million copies, organizing savings caravansca in over 15 citiesattended by over 7,000 school children, setting up the NBS Museum in our office building in KraljaPetra Street which contains educational material, publication of booklets, translation of ECBpublicationsc9.the list goes on and on and, allow me to emphasize, gives no direct benefit to theNBS, at least not in day to day terms. But, Rome was not built in a day! We have the patiencebecause we believe that we are doing the right thing. Our aim is to teach school children how tocalculate the price of a mortgage loan or to understand the meaning of an overdraft on thecurrent account instead of having to calculate only the amount of time needed to fill up ahypothetical swimming pool with water coming from two or three faucets!ca 8.caAnd, finally, there is a project which I personally favour above all else, even above givinghumanitarian aid on behalf of the National Bank, and that is participation of NBS employees inactivities such as hosting children during weekends in their homes, participation in Food Bankprojects or collecting Christmas presents for disabled children. Only we can make Serbia a betterplace, a more joyous place, a more successful place, as the activities mentioned can not, will notand should not be done by anybody else but ourselves! Let me quote our tragically killed prime minister: d2We cannot change Serbia unless we changeourselvesd3. Let us learn from each other, let us share our experiences, let us compete because thed2changingd3 will also have to be done by ourselves. Governors Office

PDF: Speech by Ruzica Stamenkovic, Director of the Solvency and Registers Division, at the 1st International Conference on Rating Central Bank Role in Rating System Development.pdf
Title: Speech at the 1st International Conference on Rating Central Bank Role in Rating System Development
text: 14/01/2009 Speech by Ruzica Stamenkovic, Director of the Solvency and RegistersDivision, at the 1st International Conference on Rating d2Central BankRole in Rating System Developmentd3 Distinguished Ladies and Gentlemen, The first international conference on rating has been organized with the purpose of highlightingthe need for developing this segment of the financial market which is still insufficientlydeveloped in our country. Eminent experts, whose presentations we have had the honour of hearing today, have introducedus to their experience in developing rating systems and different rating models. Despite the fact that a hundred years have passed since the development of the first ratingmodel, there is still no uniform approach to the rating system development and no universal rulesin designing rating models. This has also been confirmed by the presentations we have heardtoday... Traditionally, one of the roles of central banks is to preserve financial stability. During the firstsession, the speakers stressed that the key precondition for fulfilling this role is the provision offlexibility of the financial sector, along with the prevention and reduction of potential risks.Among the rest, this has also been one of the reasons for the development of rating modelswithin the framework of central banks. The representatives of Deutsche Bundesbank and Banque de France have pointed to the role ofrating within the framework of their banks, informing us that the prerequisite for thedevelopment of efficient rating models in both of these central banks has been their developedand high quality data bases. Deutsche Bundesbank started developing its rating model in 1967. Today, we heard thepresentation about their current rating model, which is used for monetary economic purposes, aswell as in the procedure of refinancing of financial institutions, and for the supervision offinancial institutions for the purpose of validation of internal rating models, and indirectly, theexternal ones. The example of Banque de France is somewhat different. In addition to its large experience inrating transactions, that it has performed in since 1982, a specific of Banque de France is that, inaddition to using the rating model for the purposes of monetary economy and supervision ofmonetary institutions, it has also used it for commercial purposes, for providing services to creditinstitutions in the procedure for credit risk assessment. As of June 2007, Banque de France hasbeen recognized as an ECAI. The second and the third sessions have pointed to the fact that the new financial marketregulations based on Basel II have introduced much stricter criteria for using internal systems formeasuring and managing credit risk, however, they have concurrently provided credit institutionswith the possibility of alternatively using the services of external credit assessment institutions(ECAIs). As regards the experience gained so far in developing internal rating models, we have beenintroduced to the details by the representatives of commercial banks, i.e. Komercijalna banka andBanca Intesa. The basic difference is in the fact that Komercijalna banka has been developing itsown model, while Banca Intesa has adjusted the internal rating model of its parent bank to theneeds of the local market. Furthermore, we have had the opportunity of learning about theexperiences of the representatives of Capp&CAPP, a rating agency now in the procedure forrecognition as an ECAI in Italy, as well as learning about the details of the requirements forobtaining that status. The Capp&CAPP representative has also pointed to the main similaritiesand differences in the procedure for solicited and unsolicited rating. The fourth session has reminded us that, in reference to rating, the association that first comesto mind is the famous international rating agencies which have a long tradition in providingrating services in the global financial market. The significance of rating was discussed by the representative of Moodyd5s, who specified that thekey benefits it provides are facilitated access to the international capital market, independentcredit risk assessment, investment portfolio diversification, as well as assistance in strategicplanning and management. The representative of Fitch Ratings pointed to an interesting fact, namely, that rating is anopinion and one of the many instruments for decision taking, but that it is not a magic productand a panacea, or a reference when it comes to purchasing or selling securities, stating also thatrating institutions do not have the role of auditors or market regulators. As regards the significance of the development of the rating system in Serbia, and potentialimplications of such development, the presentation by Professor Soskic of the Faculty ofEconomics during the fifth session introduced us to this issue in greater detail. Namely, hepointed out that credit risk monitoring and assessment has not beenca extensively implemented inour country over the past years, however, the development of the capital market, the appearanceof institutional investors and the drawing near of the moment when Basel II will have to beimplemented, necessitate the development of the rating system. Therefore, I may conclude the following d0 as regards the development of the rating system andthe rating model, there are no rules. However, as the presentations today have shown, one thingis sure, and that is the fact that the development of a rating system is an indispensableinstrument for reducing the degree of systematic risk and strengthening the stability of thefinancial market. As we have heard, different protagonists in the financial market have asignificant role in this: cacaca Central banks which, in addition to providing institutional incentives to the development ofrating, also develop data bases for credit risk measurement, on the basis of which they developand promote rating models that they use for different purposes, cacaca Commercial banks, which develop own internal rating models for their clientsd5 credit ratingassessment, or adjust the models of their parent banks to local circumstances, cacaca ECAIs, which develop external rating models for the needs of credit institutions. cacaca All in all, the process of recognition of the ECAI status is very long and complex, involvingdetailed checks of compliance with the prescribed requirements, cacaca Renowned international rating agencies which have the longest tradition in developing ratingmodels, have confirmed that their role in the international rating market has been, and willcertainly continue to be, very important. It is important to stress, here, that the latest developments in the international financial markethave raised the issue of introducing stricter regulations in this segment of the financial market,imposing the need for a more active and enhanced supervision in the future. Therefore, we are all facing a major challenge, and I believe that our todayd5s Conference has beenof help to all of us when it comes to making a step forward towards developing a modern andefficient rating system in our country. Distinguished Ladies and Gentlemen, thank you for attending this Conference in such a largenumber and I hope to see you again, next year, at our second Conference, when we shall be ableto share some new experiences about rating. Outsourced translation Governors Office

PDF: Speech of Governor Radovan Jelai at the opening of a two day meeting of the Central Committee of the International Association of Agricultural Banks, Belgrade.pdf
Title: Speech at the opening of a two day meeting of the Central Committee of the International Association of Agricultural Banks, Belgrade
text: 08/05/2009 Speech of Governor Radovan Jela.i. at the opening of a two day meetingof the Central Committee of the International Association of AgriculturalBanks, Belgrade Ladies and gentlemen, We have all been more than taken aback by the events since September last. Topics likegovernment support, pumping in money and protectionist measures have once again grabbedthe front pages worldwide and been included into d2packages of measures to counter negativeeffects of the economic crisisd3 and incorporated into many other ideas and suggestions. But before addressing the main issue, allow me to make some general remarks. 1) I am surprised to see that there are so many advocates of J.M. Keynes and wonder if anyonehas read his theory through to realize that one needs to save during good times, such as thosewe had during the last decade, i.e. to conduct counter-cyclical instead of pro-cyclical fiscal policy.We see that nowadays almost everybody is competing to increase public spending. But, there isone major difference that we should be aware of d0 some countries can afford it or have access tocheap money in the market, while that alternative remains closed to others, as is the case ofSerbia. 2) Besides, very few advocates of fiscal expansion think in terms of a time horizon longer than 2to 3 years. Should however even central banks decide not to think about it, things could get reallytroublesome. Regardless of whether credit expansion is generated by the World Bank or the IMFor the EU d0 a credit represents an additional source of finance and is not an adjustment d0 andadjustment is what is really needed now.ca Whether and to what extent will the world ever go backto the time before the crisis, yet remains to be seen. 3) Due to pending fundamental changes in the world economy, economic models applied by thecountries in transition need to be urgently changed d0 credit supplied by international financialinstitutions can provide some form of assistance but there is no way that macroeconomic issuesexperienced by these countries can be resolved through additional borrowing. The d2welfaresocietyd3 has been built too soon and has encompassed too many countries still undergoingtransition processes. To a certain extent, these countries went ahead of their time and now haveto consolidate their finances. This is not going to be easy or cheap, and most certainly notpopular. What is our position with regard to the place and the role of the central bank in the context ofmaintaining economic stability? Allow me to mention six categories only, though the list could bemuch extended: 1) Preserving price stability remains our objective above all else. Let us remind ourselves thatSerbian economy, like so many others, has proved to be competent of generating even two-digitinflation despite declining growth in the social product. 2) Supply of additional liquidity to the banking sector, because liquidity is the most obvious signof the stability in the banking sector. Even now, we still hold substantial amounts of deposits inNBS repo securities, which in the dinar counter value exceed EUR 1 billion, while banks haveaccess to additional funds from the NBS against the collateral in government securities ormortgage loans. 3) Securing solvency levels in the banking sector during the period of weakening domesticcurrency and borrowing in foreign currency requires constant vigilance in terms of compliancewith capital adequacy requirements. It is therefore most commending that the NBS is going toconduct stress testing of top 10 Serbian banks in order to secure that those with insufficientcapital are recapitalized. 4) Drafting central bank measures so as to prevent substantial withdrawal of capital from thecountry. An agreement has been reached with top ten banks not to decrease their creditexposure to Serbia. 5) The NBS keeps relaxing its supervision-related legislation but obviously not fast enough sincebanks have been tightening their policy in sync. And as the NBS has been taking measures totighten control ever since the transition began, banks were relaxing their policies. The processesnow seem to have reversed. 6) Support to Government programs d0 unless contrary to our primary objective of preserving pricestability d0 the NBS shall support the measures taken by the government. That is what we havebeen doing so far and that is what we will keep doing in future. Times ahead are full of uncertainties and shall be a testing period in all aspects. But it is ourdemocracy that will be put to the greatest test and we shall soon see if, and to what extent, wehave managed to build one.ca I hope we shall pass that test too, and shall not forget that thechallenges facing us now cannot be resolved through economic populist measures, derogation ofinstitutions and changes in regulatory framework. Adjustment, which appears even moreimportant in the light of the global economic crisis, means that Serbia must act more decisivelyand be more efficient in doing what it has delayed to do during good times in order to maintainmacroeconomic and financial stability and secure chances of development once the d2stormd3 hassubsided. Governors Office

PDF: Governor Jelais Address to Members of Parliament about Draft Amendments to the Law on the National Bank of Serbia.pdf
Title: Governor Jelais Address to Members of Parliament about Draft Amendments to the Law on the National Bank of Serbia
text: 12/06/2010 Governor Jela.i.d5s Address to Members of Parliament about DraftAmendments to the Law on the National Bank of Serbia Dear Madam Speaker, dear Members of Parliament, You have before you the text of Draft Amendments to the Law on the National Bank of Serbia,proposed by the National Bank of Serbia with a view to harmonising the Law with theConstitution of the Republic of Serbia and strengthening central bank independence in line withcentral banking standards, as well as principles and recommendations of international financialinstitutions (the European Central Bank, International Monetary Fund, World Bank). In addition,we also aimed to eliminate irregularities and clarify the provisions whose implementation poseddilemmas (primarily those relating to capital, coverage of losses, allocation of profit and theStatute). The amendments will also provide for further harmonisation with the Treaty on theEuropean Union and the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, particularly with theprovisions of the Statute of the European System of Central Banks and of the European CentralBank d0 in view of the Republic of Serbiad5s strategic commitment to join the European Union. The key novelties in the Law are the following: cacaca strengthening all four main aspects of National Bank of Serbiad5s independence and autonomy d0functional, institutional, personnel and financial; cacaca setting up the Executive Board that will take over all responsibilities of the Monetary PolicyCommittee and a part of Governord5s responsibilities in the domain of financial sector supervision; cacaca improvement of the supervisory role of the Governord5s Council of the National Bank of Serbia; ca cacaca clarification of provisions on the election, termination of office and the conflict of interest ofthe Governor, Vice-Governors and members of the Council; cacaca introduction of more comprehensive and clear provisions on monetary policy instruments andother functions of the National Bank of Serbia; cacaca prohibition of public sector financing; cacaca precise definition of National Bank of Serbiad5s assets and the manner of allocating its profitand covering losses; cacaca upgrade of the accountability system for the purpose of strengthening corporate governance inthe National Bank of Serbia; cacaca more detailed regulation of other organisational and internal issues. It should be noted that the principle of central bank independence and autonomy is not anobjective per se, but a means of reaching the bankd5s primary objective d0 the achievement andmaintenance of price stability. The first, functional aspect of independence implies unambiguous prioritising of objectives d0 theprimary objective remains the achievement and maintenance of price stability. One of theobjectives prescribed is the maintenance of the financial sector as well. Furthermore, theresponsibility of the National Bank of Serbiad5s bodies for the achievement of these objectives hasbeen clearly defined d0 the Executive Board and the Governor, within their respective remits, areresponsible for the achievement of objectives and the Council is in charge of supervision. Secondly, with the aim of strengthening the institutional independence of the National Bank ofSerbia, the Bank, its bodies and members of its bodies cannot seek or take instructions fromgovernment bodies and organisations or from any other person, nor can government bodies andorganisations or other persons jeopardise the Bankd5s independence and autonomy or seek toinfluence the Bank, its bodies and members of its bodies in the performance of their tasks. Therelationship with government bodies has been defined in a way that ensures their mutualcooperation and does not jeopardise the National Bank of Serbiad5s independence. The amendments regarding Governord5s election arrangements, extended term of office of theGovernor, Vice-Governors and members of the Council (from five to six years), the procedure ofcompulsory retirement of these persons and the unequivocal right to judicial examination of thedecision on compulsory retirement are likely to contribute to the personnel independence of theNational Bank of Serbia, i.e. they are likely to prevent the influence of government bodies on theperformance of the Bankd5s tasks. On the other hand, the provisions stipulating the prevention ofthe conflict of interest exclude the influence of other persons, particularly those supervised bythe National Bank of Serbia and/or those it cooperates with. Finally, the financial independence, which underlies all other aspects of central bankindependence, is provided in provisions clearly stipulating that the National Bank of Serbia, forthe purpose of achieving the objectives and performing the tasks envisaged by the Law, shouldbe independent in establishing its revenues and expenditures and should have its own assets, aswell as in provisions prescribing new rules on capital, allocation of profit and coverage of losses. I would like to underscore that strengthening of the National Bank of Serbiad5s independence andautonomy does not exclude cooperation with economic policy creators, but places thiscooperation on more clear and legally firmer grounds, contributing not only to better qualitycoordination, but to more efficient implementation of economic policy as well. At the same time,strengthened independence and autonomy of the central bank implies its greater responsibilityfor the measures and decisions taken and implies the need for greater transparency of its work,which is why the Law prescribes more frequent reporting to the National Assembly (the FinancialStability Report, semi-annual report on monetary policy, etc). As regards management of National Bank of Serbiad5s operations and supervision of itsoperations, the new provisions reallocate the responsibilities of bodies. The Executive Board willassume greater responsibility in the field of preserving and strengthening the stability of thefinancial sector and the Bankd5s supervisory function, as well as the responsibility for regulatingimportant issues pertaining to the Bankd5s operations (the tariff, assets, proposing the Statuteand the Bankd5s development strategy, etc) which have so far generally fallen under the Governord5sremit. The Governord5s Council will also assume additional responsibilities, particularly in thesphere of financial operations, which are to contribute to better quality and more efficientsupervision of the National Bank of Serbia. At the end, I would like to mention a novelty regarding the prohibition of monetary financing. TheLaw contains a provision prohibiting the central bank to finance public authorities, regardless ofthe level of authority (Republic, regional or local level) and the form of authority (directly orindirectly in the form of public enterprises, agencies or other legal entities that it founded or inwhich it has a controlling stake). This provision is of key importance for the achievement of theprimary objective of monetary policy and for the maintenance of indispensable fiscal discipline. Thank you very much for your attention. I stand ready to answer any of your questions about thedraft amendments to the Law which will contribute in the long run to the upgrade of operationsof the Republic of Serbiad5s central bank, the achievement of its objectives and to the well-beingof our country! Title: Governor Jelai's Speech
text: 02/07/2010 Governor Jela.i.'s Speech Jubilees are a good opportunity to look back and reflect on what we have done in the past year.The National Bank of Serbiad5s task is not only to dampen excessive and unrealistic expectationswhen times are good, but also to provide a dose of realism now when most tend to seeeverything through dark lenses. Even in times of crisis, the National Bank of Serbia has managed to accomplish its principal legalmandate, which is to achieve and maintain price stability, as well as to preserve stability of thefinancial sector. We have to admit that in terms of maintaining price stability we were aided byexternal factors, but even more by the unpopular adjustment measures taken by the Governmentof the Republic of Serbia such as the freeze on wages and pensions, public spending cuts,keeping taxes on hold, etc. All of these measures proved once again that, irrespective of thedegree of euroisation, the factor determining prices in Serbia is not the exchange rate, but therelationship between demand and supply. Inflation has been put under control and does notmirror movements in the exchange rate. In June, it is expected to measure around 4% y-o-y.Unlike the recent past, when prices were raised practically over night, both businessmen andtraders now listen to the voices of the market, price increases are announced to test consumerresponse, and finally, if such price increases do take place, they are usually lower than originallyannounced. I am not trying to say that inflation expectations are no longer high d0 what else couldthey be after several decades of inflationary habits and business psychology? What I am trying tosay is that now it has been brought home to everybody that prices depend not only on supply, butincreasingly on demand as well. I have to admit that I am a bit surprised that only d2halfd3 of allproducers and traders are now planning to increase their prices d0 I thought all of them wouldwant to!!! In terms of financial sector, allow me to underscore that its stability has been sustained despitean increase in NPLs. We have just finished the stress testing based on banksd5 data as at 31March. The results of the stress tests have shown that even in the downside macroeconomicscenario, the capital adequacy ratio of the banking sector, that currently stands at 21.5%, woulddecline to 16.8% at end-2011 and still hold high above the regulatory minimum. This means thatthe financial stability is guaranteed. The stress testing has proved that the banking sector isresilient to both external and internal shocks and that there is no need for extraordinary, pre-emptive recapitalisation of banks. Looking at the broader macroeconomic picture, we may argue that Serbia is on the right track d0learning lessons from the crisis that will serve as a foundation for its economic recovery and long-term sustainable development. Though under coercion, our economy is undergoing restructuringand its growth is increasingly based on exports rather than domestic demand, which is currentlyvery low with the freeze on wages and pensions in place, significantly lower credit growth,weaker cross-border borrowing and declining public consumption. This is best illustrated by thefact that from January through May this year, for the first time ever, Serbiad5s export/import coverratio reached 65%, implying that export capable businesses are looking increasingly tointernational markets that we had lost literally over night and that will be difficult to regain. Yes, Serbia will come out of this crisis with a significantly higher public debt, but this will not dragus into a debt crisis quagmire. What matters is that we reduce our public debt until some futureturmoil of our own or international making arises, since the crisis always entails a liquiditysqueeze, a significant increase in the price of capital and a decrease in tax revenue. The questionis what we will do once economic prosperity is restored. Whether we will be running budgetdeficits just because of the greater scope for their financing? What will we spend our one-offprivatisation receipts on, etc? In their historical review of state bankruptcies over the past 200years, economic analysts Kenneth Rogoff and Carmen Reinhart argue that the real capacity of acountry and its economy is more important than the current level of the debt it runs. Theirresearch shows that public debt rises on average by 86% during the first three years of the crisis,but also that the share of public debt in GDP in more than half of the countries that wentbankrupt was less than 60%, or less than 40% in nearly 20% of those countries. In the comingseveral years, public debt to GDP ratio will, no doubt, play a crucial role in setting risk premiumsand margins for individual countries. We see now how important it was that Serbia turned to the IMF in time and that its positiveeconomic performance was endorsed by the completed fourth review under Serbiad5s Stand-ByArrangement. This gives Serbia not only access to cheap sources of finance to cover its deficit,but also boosts its rating in the eyes of foreign investors, international financial institutions andthe EU. Unlike some other countries, Serbia, for the time being, need not look for rescue ininternational financial markets that have been practically closed for the past several weeks d0 thespreads are no longer an issue as money is virtually gone. Negative macroeconomic developments in the region are rather worrying as these countries areour key trade partners. In the last year alone, we recorded a surplus with Montenegro of EUR 476million, Bosnia and Herzegovina EUR 412 million, and Macedonia EUR 140 million. Moreover, thecrisis has taught us that no country is an island, meaning that financial, commodity and tradeflows intertwine, bringing both positive and negative developments alongside. For instance, thesuccess of the tourist season in Montenegro and the potential inflow of foreign capital willdepend on our exchange rate and the living standard that will impact on the number of ourtourists visiting Montenegro and the amount of money they will spend. Furthermore, the future of the banking sector, particularly the level of lending, is an issue forserious consideration. Though banks are stable and liquid and lending grows by around 10% p.a.in real terms, the problem arises as to the sources of fresh lending on the medium run. Today,when wages and pensions are frozen we cannot expect any major increases in sources of bankfinancing in the domestic market. Moreover, conditions in international financial markets are nottoo promising, while the demand stays strong! The National Bank of Serbia celebrates its jubilee today with an exhibition devoted to anotherjubilee d0 the 160th anniversary of birth of Georg Weifert, the Governor who served the longest(26 years!) and who left a personal imprint on the history of our central bank. Joining theinitiative for this year to be marked as a year dedicated to Weifert, the National Bank has issued20-dinar memorial coins featuring Weifertd5s portrait. I warmly invite you all to see the exhibitiond2Life and Times of Georg Weifertd3, which will show us that each time has its own challenges,while the value of an individual and credibility of an institution are measured in terms of thecapacity to overcome these challenges. Esteemed representatives of the financial sector! I wish to thank you all for the continuedsupport, advice and criticism over the last ten years that I have spent in the National Bank ofSerbia. It is not easy to leave. This institution is almost like a magnet in that it attracts first-classexperts and associates. Let others talk of what I have accomplished in the first decade of thiscentury. I am particularly glad that this institution has proved its strength yet again by having thegovernord5s relay passed without much ado, without speculations, back-corridors talk and politicalshenigans. We are seeing here, as the matter of fact, quite a natural and d0 let me underscore d0 atruly democratic transfer of power. This is what I have been fighting for in the past 10 years andwhat I have obviously succeeded in achieving. ca I thank you all very much indeed! National Bank of Serbia

Title: Speech at the Bankar Magazine Roundtable
text: 02/11/2010 Speech by Mr Veselin Pjescic, General Manager of the Monetary Systemand Policy Department at the Bankar Magazine Roundtable e3IMPORTANCE OF DOMESTIC SAVINGS FOR THE NEW MODEL OFECONOMIC GROWTHd2 The increase in savings as a source of investment financing is essential for Serbiad5s long-termsustainable economic growth. It is only by increasing domestic savings, government and privatealike, that the scope can be created for non-inflationary investment growth needed to accelerateeconomic recovery. The capacity of the domestic economy to boost savings is not only one of thekey prerequisites to step up economic growth, but also to preserve stability of themacroeconomic environment. The general impression is that the current level of savings is rather low. Estimates for 2010suggest that national savings1 make up around 11% of GDP2, the world average being around23%3. At the same time, the volume of savings in Serbia is lower than in other countries andregions. In Central-East Europe, savings account for 17% of GDP4. African countries alsooutperform Serbia in this respect, while developing Asia boasts a savings to GDP ratio of as muchas 44%5. On the other hand, estimated at around 19%6, the share of investment in Serbiad5s GDPis lower than the world average of around 23%7. The gap between higher investment and lowernational savings results in a net inflow of foreign savings, i.e. deficit on the current account.What sets Serbia apart from other countries is not the level of investment or the current accountdeficit, but a relatively low level of savings. This, however, does not mean that the level ofinvestment is satisfactory. As Serbiad5s economic growth and the speed of convergence toadvanced economies depend on investment, its quantity in Serbia should be much higher thanthe world average. Let us remind ourselves that some transition countries recorded in certainstages of transition an investment to GDP ratio8 of more than 30%. The pre-crisis economic growth model was based on low domestic savings and abundant foreigncapital inflow, either in the form of FDI or direct cross-border borrowing. What often comes handin hand with a low volume of domestic savings are low investment and a high external currentaccount deficit. Being heavily reliant on the inflow of foreign savings, this model of growth mayultimately result in high foreign indebtedness of the domestic economy. With the outbreak of theglobal economic crisis, all the downsides to running serious foreign trade and current accountdisbalances came to the fore.ca Contracted inflow of foreign capital and strained access tointernational sources of financing, accompanied with sharp depreciation pressures, revealed thetrue scope of vulnerability of the Serbian economy. In the new circumstances, reducing consumption and increasing domestic savings is the only wayto boost investment without giving rise to higher current account deficit and excessive foreignborrowing. To achieve long-term sustainable economic growth, the pattern of increasingconsumption that is not covered by the growth in GDP must be abandoned. Under the baselinescenario of the Serbian Post-Crisis Economic Growth and Development Model 2011-20209, toachieve 5.8% average GDP growth until 2020, the share of investment in GDP must increase to25% by 2015 and to 28% by 2020, while the share of consumption must be cut from 92.5% in2011 to 81% in 2020.ca At the same time, national savings should reach 23.6% of GDP by 2015and 27.7% by 2020. Export-oriented development strategy implies an increase in the export toGDP ratio from 27.6% in 2009 to 65% in 2020, and a cut in the current account deficit to 3.3% ofGDP at the end of the period observed. To get back on the path of long-term sustainable economic growth, Serbia must increase boththe volume of savings and investment. The question arises as to what steps need to be taken toactually propel savings. As economic policy cannot impact on private savings in the short run, allstakes are placed on impacting government savings. Economic policy makers are called on to takeunpopular and painful measures that will ultimately result in increased domestic savings. Thesemeasures include a sweeping reform of the public sector and the pension system, expected toinduce a decrease in the share of public consumption in GDP. Lower share of public consumptionin GDP should indirectly lead to a rise in private savings, by way of increasing disposable incomeof the private sector. On the other hand, the National Bank of Serbia is taking measures, withinits remit, to preserve macroeconomic and price stability, as well as stability of the financialsystem, these being prerequisites for the increase in any type of savings at all. ca One of the key challenges ahead of the National Bank of Serbia is to reduce the level ofeuroisation, i.e. to increase the dinarisation of the domestic economy. As the global economiccrisis and the depreciation of the dinar set in, high financial euroisation and heavy reliance onforeign sources of funding deepened the disproportion in the size of the unhedged governmentand private sector balance sheets. Dinarisation is a long-term process of gradual adjustment onthe assets and liabilities side of banking sector balance sheet, which should reinforce theefficiency of monetary policy and ease the vulnerability of the Serbian economy to currencychanges. The National Bank of Serbia is determined to encourage the process of dinarisationthrough, for the time being, indirect and market-based measures. The dinarisation strategy is envisaged to be implemented by all financial stakeholders: theNational Bank of Serbia, the banking sector, the government, and the public. It rests on threeinter-connected pillars. The first pillar of the dinarisation strategy implies the strengthening ofthe macroeconomic environment by delivering low and stable inflation through a flexibleexchange rate, alongside durable economic growth and stable financial system. The second pillarconsists of activities creating favourable conditions for the development of long-term dinarsecurities market and an actively traded dinar yield curve. The third pillar of the dinarisationstrategy aims to promote FX hedging instruments and their use. Strengthening the resilience of the domestic financial system must be based on the greater useof the dinar. This calls for a number of activities d0 ranging from the implementation of inflationtargeting regime to educating borrowers about the FX risk. One of the measures taken by theNational Bank of Serbia with a view to encouraging the use of the dinar is the exemption fromreserve requirements of time dinar savings accumulated during the so-called Savings Week. Thisis a good example of a measure geared at promoting dinar savings and, at the same time,contributing to the process of dinarisation. In addition to this, over the past several months theNational Bank of Serbia took a number of steps aiming to contribute to the dinarisation of thedomestic financial system: it abolished collateral deposit requirement for dinar loans; raised theborrowing limit for citizens from 30% to 40% of their monthly income provided minimum 80% ofdebt is dinar-denominated; lowered the dinar reserve requirement ratio from 10% to 5%;launched a public campaign to raise awareness of the need for FX hedging and organised a set ofconferences on the subject. The government has also contributed to the dinarisation process,notably by issuing t-bills of longer maturities (18 and 24 months) and by subsidising only dinarliquidity and consumer loans. The assets side of the banking sector balance sheet is already showing the results of thedinarisation process. The share of dinar in total lending to the household and corporate sectorsrose from 24.6% in March to 29% in September. On the liabilities side, however, there is still nochange in the currency composition of savings though, according to the National Bank of Serbiad5sanalyses, holding dinars in savings accounts mostly paid off better than holding foreign exchangeover the last ten years10. As earlier said, it will take years of sustainable macroeconomic and financial stability to fosterthe expected growth in private dinar savings, but this growth will come about gradually, as aresult of concerted efforts of the government, the National Bank of Serbia and the bankingsector. The National Bank of Serbia will also give its contribution to creating a favourableinvestment environment, as well as to preserving a safe and sound banking sector and tostrengthening the institutions offering alternative types of investment and savings (for instance,life insurance, voluntary pension funds, etc), all of this leading to an increase in domestic savings. text: NATIIONALBANKOF SERRBIA Vice Governor Markovis speech at the presentation of the May 2011 Inflation Report Belgradde, 18 May 2011 Esteemed members of the press and fellow economists, welcome to the presentation of the May Inflation Report. After temporary slowdown in Q4 2010, economic recovery resumed in Q1 2011.We expect the recovery to continue at a moderate pace, accompanied with structural adjustment of GDP from consumption towards investment, and a reduction of external imbalances. The strongest contribution to GDP growth in 2011 should come from investments, bolstered by improved domestic and international economic recovery prospects. On the other hand, despite the unfreezing of public sector wages, high unemployment will hold back household consumption, making its contribution to GDP positive, but rather modest. The contribution of net exports will continue to be positive, although lower than in the previous period, partly due to the real appreciation of the dinar, but also due to the expected growth in imports of capital and intermediate goods spurred by economic rebound. In the meantime, inflation came at 14.7% in April, which was in line with NBS expectations. After peaking in April or May, inflation is expected to start retreating towards the target, and to return within the tolerance band in H1 2012.Through its tight monetary policy in the previous period, the NBS aimed to return the inflation within the target band gradually and sustainably, while minimizing negative effects on economic activity and employment. In addition to monetary policy measures, inflations return to the target is supported by stable inflation expectations and low aggregate demand, as well as by the gradual easing of inflationary pressures from food prices, which were the main driving force behind inflation growth in the prior period. In this speech, we will present our view of past inflation and macroeconomic developments, explain monetary policy measures taken by the NBS, set out the expected profile for inflation and economic growth in the coming period, and outline monetary policy measures to be taken by the NBS in accordance with those expectations. INFLATION AND MACROECONOMIC DEVELOPMENTS Inflation in Q1 2011 came at 5.5%, while food price grew by 10.6%. Processed food prices rose by 8.0%, mainly due to cost.push pressures from the rising prices of primary agricultural products, such as corn and wheat. Fruit and vegetable prices recorded a particularly strong growth of 25.3%, which is significantly above the seasonal pattern for this part of the year. But in the long run, it represents the basis for the sustainable economic development. Strengthening of the dinar against the euro, in place since December 2010, continued in the first four months of 2011. The only safe way for companies and households to protect themselves against possible negative consequences of FX fluctuations is to borrow in the currency of their income, or to use FX hedging instruments. Over the last year, the impact of exchange rate volatility on the corporate and household sectors has diminished. Additionally, almost half of new loans in this period were extended in dinars (without an FX indexation clause), meaning that shifts in the exchange rate will not affect those borrowers. As indicated by both components of the monetary conditions index, monetary policy is assessed to have become restrictive in Q1 2011. First, strengthening of the dinar in early 2011, and higher inflation, prompted real appreciation and opened the appreciation gap. At the same time, the real key policy rate rose above its trend, which declined due to falling country risk premium. Despite the restrictive measures taken by the NBS over the past eight months, inflation will remain above the upper bound of the target band until end.2011, and is expected to retreat within the band in H1 2012. This may raise the question as to why the central bank did not react more aggressively. To answer this question, one should first underline that the NBSs inflation target is set continuously, for each month of the year, and not just for a year.end, as it is sometimes wrongly interpreted by the public. Hence, achieving the inflation target, for instance, in March or June, is equally important to the NBS as in December. Though price stability is NBSs primary objective, it should be underscored that the monetary policy task in an inflation targeting regime is not to keep inflation on target at all times. Price adjustments are often a necessary element in reaction to supply.side shocks, such as the last years food shock. The central banks task in an inflation targeting regime is to respond using all instruments at its disposal to cushion the effects of either inflationary or disinflationary price shocks, and to bring inflation back to the target as quickly as possible, but in a sustainable and stable manner. Box 1 of the Inflation Report illustrates different inflation paths, resulting from different monetary policy reactions to an inflationary shock. An adequate monetary policy reaction, as opposed to a very aggressive one, would result in inflation returning to the target band somewhat later after the initial shock, but after coming close to the target inflation would remain there in the medium term. In case of a very aggressive reaction, inflation would return to the target band more swiftly. However, due to the monetary policy lag, such a reaction usually results in significant undershooting, as well as volatility, and the ensuing much later stabilisation around the target. Had the NBS raised the key policy rate more aggressively in H2 2010 and early 2011, it could have brought about faster return of inflation within the target band. First,theinflationprojectiondrawsontheassumptionofanaverageagriculturalseasonthis year,implyingamoderatedeclineinagriculturalproductprices,thoughnottheirreturnto theearly.2010levels.Basedonthat,inflationisexpectedtoretreatwithinthetargetbandin H1 2012. In case of another exceptionally weak agricultural season, agricultural product prices would probably not decline and inflations retreat within the target band would be slower. On the contrary, in case the agricultural season turns out well, these prices could decline much more swiftly, and inflation would fall back within the target band more rapidly. The second risk stems from movements in Serbias risk premiumthat reflects investors trust in the country. Risk premium fluctuated strongly throughout 2010  it rose from May in response to the sovereign debt crisis in some euro zone member states, triggering depreciation pressures on the dinar, only to decline by end.2010 and early 2011, fuelling appreciation pressures. Surprises in this regard cannot be fully disregarded, and could affect the speed of inflations return to the target. The third risk concerns the fiscal policy role in maintaining macroeconomic stability. Any stronger exceeding of the planned fiscal deficit would elevate demand.side inflationary pressures, but could also spur a renewed rise in risk premium and capital flight, causing depreciation pressures and inflations slower return to the target. On the other hand, keeping the fiscal deficit within the planned limit would underpin the projected inflations return to the target. On balance, risks to the projection are slightly skewed to the upside. Based on the inflation projection and its underlying risks, the Executive Board judges that the key policy rate is either close to, or at the peak of its current cycle. To keep inflation within the target band in the medium term, the NBS will probably continue implementing tight monetary policy, using all instruments of monetary regulation available. Finally, allow me to reiterate our confidence that high inflation rates will not persist over an extended period, and that we expect inflation to return within the target band until the middle of the next year. Thank you for your attention.

Title: Speech on the Research development strategy of the National Bank of Serbia
text: 24/06/2011 Speech of Vice-Governor Bojan Markovi. "Research developmentstrategy of the National Bank of Serbia" Belgrade, 23 June 2011 Research development strategy of the National Bank of Serbia Todayd5s conference is part of the National Bank of Serbiad5s strategy aimed at improving theeconomic profession and research in the field of economics and finance in Serbia. It is ourambition to make Belgrade a place where it will be possible to learn, follow the latestdevelopments and work on state-of-the-art aspects of modern economic science. We wish toshow to you d0 young people attending PhD and Masterd5s courses at prestigious universitiesworldwide and at home, that the National Bank of Serbia implements and develops seriousresearch activities. This may entice you to come back to your country one day or to see in ourinstitution a chance for your further professional development. What is indispensable in an inflation targeting monetary regime is a continuous upgrade of themethodology used in making the most important strategic decisions, which requires cutting-edge economic knowledge. This is the principle upheld by the European Central Bank, centralbanks of the UK, Canada, Australia, and all developed economies in the world running inflationtargeting regimes. The National Bank of Serbia was guided by the same principle in designing itslong-term activities aimed at raising the level of scientific economic research in Serbia and thedevelopment of its research potentials. This will certainly enhance the National Bank of Serbiad5sreputation both in the country and the world. Greater credibility of a central bank leads to betteranchored inflation expectations and greater monetary policy efficiency. The National Bank of Serbia has already started to implement its research development strategy.The Chief Economistd5s Office was set up, tasked with establishing the priority research directions.We aspire to turn the National Bank of Serbia into a knowledge centre that will gather arespectable research team operating in line with the highest international standards. I stronglybelieve the National Bank can be transformed into a centre of economic scientific thought both inthe region and Europe. We have designed the First Conference of Young Serbian Economists as a forum where youngpeople can present their research papers before a professional public and further improve themthrough interaction with top-notch Serbian economists such as professor Bojan Jovanovi. who iswith us today. I would like to use this opportunity and announce that the National Bank will soon step up itsissue of working papers, thus contributing to the spread of knowledge and helping economicpolicy creators in decision making. In this way the Bank will receive feedback from the globaleconomic community and enable the authors of these papers to publish them in professionaljournals. We also plan to intensify the ongoing education of employees by organising training in key skills,such as risk analysis, monetary policy models and financial supervision. Each Friday, the National Bank hosts research seminars held by leading economists such as BojanJovanovi., Lucrezia Reichlin, Bernard Dumas, Charles Engel, Jordi Gal92, Fabrizio Zilibotti and manyother world-renowned names. We believe the National Bank of Serbia staff should have regularcontact with best world economists, communicate with them, discuss lecturersd5 and their ownpapers, as well as National Bankd5s projects that they work on. Through an upgrade in research resources, a high quality professional library, special databases,economic analysis software, etc, we wish to enable research staff in the Bank to engage inscientific work in accordance with the highest world standards. ca Within this long-term strategy, the National Bank of Serbia plans to organise internationalconferences that are relevant for its research activities. Along with strengthening our reputation,we aim to attract some of the most eminent foreign experts in particular fields, young peoplefrom Serbia with significant potential, as well as practicing researchers. We are currently discussing with the Center for Economic and Policy Research (CEPR) theorganisation of one of its 2012 conferences in Belgrade. In March 2012, our capital city will hostthe annual meeting of the Bank for International Settlements Working Group on monetary policy. We shall devote special attention to the development of institutional cooperation with centralbanks and international academic and other institutions. Such cooperation will involve joint workon research projects, the exchange of research study visits, joint exploitation of researchresources, cooperation in organisation of research seminars. Through the d2guest researcherd3concept and organisation of advanced courses on a par with PhD courses delivered at leadingworld universities, we intend to bring to the National Bank distinguished researchers and enablecooperation with them. For instance, Peter Sinclair, a professor at Oxford and Birminghamuniversities will hold in a few days time a master course in macroeconomics. The National Bank has decided to issue special awards to stimulate the development of scientificeconomic thought in and about Serbia. It has established an annual financial award for youngscientists from the country and region for the best scientific-expert work on monetary policy,financial supervision or financial stability. The award will be given based on a competitionlaunched by the National Bank. An annual award will also be given for the best PhD thesis defended at a Serbian university in thefields of macroeconomics, finance, monetary economics, supervision or financial stability. Thebest Masterd5s theses on macroeconomics and finance, written in Serbia in the previous year, willalso be eligible for a special annual award. These awards are intended for those doing research inSerbia. Moreover, to stimulate research on Serbia, we have also established an annual award for the bestanalytical research paper in the field of macroeconomics, based on Serbian data. The award isalso intended for authors abroad who conduct research on Serbia. ca This is only a part of the strategy aimed at upgrading the economic profession and research inthis field, which the National Bank of Serbia has recently begun to implement. We aim tointroduce into our work and our environment the highest professional and scientific standardsand to turn the National Bank of Serbia into a knowledge nucleus that will expand across Serbiaand be respected throughout the world. I hope that some of you will soon become a part of our team. Governor's Office

Over the past weeks we have witnessed turbulence in the global financial markets, stemming primarily from sovereign debt crises in some advanced economies and currency zones. Growing pessimism has led to a sharp downfall in stock indexes across the world, pushed up the prices of gold and sent down international prices of primary commodities. All of this has heightened uncertainties with regard to the pace of further economic recovery at home. With the world facing a sovereign debt crisis, the markets will be particularly sensitive to the conduct of fiscal policy and the implementation of the planned budget framework. According to preliminary estimates, following strong growth in the first quarter, economic activity grew by 2.2% y.o.y in the second quarter, while stagnating q.o.q. Still, we expect that the weaker performance in the second quarter will be compensated for by stronger growth in the second half of the year, mainly because of good agricultural performance. Therefore our projection for GDP growth has remained unchanged from May Inflation Report, i.e. in 2011 we expect growth of around 3%. As expected by the National Bank of Serbia, the new agricultural season has led to lower food prices and weaker inflationary pressure on that account. We expect inflation to continue to fall, gaining particular momentum from August to November due to the base effect. We expect that the next time we meet here, at the presentation of the November Inflation Report,y.o.y inflation will be in single digits, and that it will return within the target tolerance band in the first half of 2012. In addition to lower inflationary pressures from food prices, the drop in inflation will be aided by the restrictive monetary policy measures taken in the prior period, by the low aggregate demand and the likely drop in inflation expectations. Assessing that inflationary pressures are receding, the National Bank has started a monetary policy easing cycle in June, lowering the key policy rate since then by a total of 0.75 pp to its current level of 11.75%. In its August meeting, the NBS Executive Board decided to keep the key policy rate on hold in order to get a better insight into the effects of recent turmoil in global financial markets. Today we will present our view of past inflation and macroeconomic developments, explain monetary policy measures taken by the NBS, set out the expected outlook for inflation and economic growth in the coming period, and outline monetary policy measures to be taken by the NBS in accordance with those expectations. INFLATION AND MACROECONOMIC DEVELOPMENTS The second quarter of 2011 saw a turnaround in movement of food prices and a drop in the associated inflationary pressures. Inflation fell from 5.5% in the first quarter to 1.2% in the second quarter, or in y.o.y terms, from 14.1% in March to 12.7% in June, which is at the lower end of our fan chart from the May Inflation Report. The new agricultural season brought about a decrease in fruit and vegetable prices already in the second quarter, which is atypical for that time of the year. This is due to the fact fruit and vegetable prices were exceptionally high at the start of the new season, and to good weather conditions favourable to agricultural production. As there are no official announcements of major administered price revisions in the near term, no significant growth in these prices is likely in the second half of the year. In line with our expectations, y.o.y inflation continued to fall in July, settling at 12.1%. At monthly level, consumer prices dropped 0.5% on the back of the 14.7% seasonal decrease in fruit and vegetable prices recorded in July. Since the start of the global economic crisis, the sources of GDP growth have been shifting away from domestic demand, both final and investment, towards net external demand. Thus, exports in June were 9% higher and imports 21% lower than their pre.crisis levels. In 2011 and in the years beyond, we expect that the strongest contribution to economic growth will come from fixed investment and net exports. This is essential for sustainable long.term growth. Investments in automobile industry represent a good example in this context. By 2016 these investments could add around 2 pp to GDP growth on a cumulative basis, primarily by boosting exports. This is discussed in Text box 1 of the August Inflation Report. The Text box also presents an estimate that the announced investments in automobile industry would cut the share of current account deficit in GDP by around 1.5 pp per year during the period observed. After strengthening from November through May, the dinar weakened slightly over the past two months. Unlike the previous years, its weakening was not accompanied by the slide in interbank foreign exchange market trading volumes.
