Daily volatility of the dinar exchange rate increased during this period, but still remained lower than that exhibited by other currencies with a floating exchange rate, such as the Polish zloty, Hungarian forint and Turkish lira, and we expect such tendencies will persist in the coming period as well. The deepening of the interbank foreign exchange market and a somewhat greater daily volatility of the exchange rate of the dinar should have a positive impact on the use of FX hedging instruments and the process of dinarisation. It should also lead to a shift in the structure of capital inflows towards longer.term flows, which will strengthen the stability of the market and, by extension, alleviate exchange rate volatility in the medium run. As a consequence of restrictive measures taken until April, the degree of monetary policy restrictiveness increased in the second quarter. This was primarily due to the widening of the appreciation gap in the second quarter as a result of nominal strengthening of the dinar. On the other hand, with respect to the real interest rate, the degree of restrictiveness was approximately the same as in the first quarter. In view of developments over the last two months, the appreciation gap of the real exchange rate has narrowed in the meantime. This implies that the exchange rate factored by net importers in their products is probably higher than its current level. As indicated by the negative output gap, low aggregate demand will generate disinflationary pressures in the medium run. As the economy recovers, the disinflationary impact of this factor will weaken. A decline in inflation in the coming months is likely to bring down inflation expectations, meaning that the related inflationary pressures might weaken, thereby lending a further impetus to the disinflation process. Following a vigorous rise in the first half of 2011, administered prices will rise much more moderately during the remaining months of the year. This notwithstanding, administered price growth in 2011 will overshoot the planned limit of 7b12%, and will reach, according to our current estimates, around 11.6%. In addition to monthly rates, the path of y.o.y inflation in the coming period will be largely determined by the so.called base effect, i.e. monthly inflation rates in the corresponding period of the previous year. As last yeard5s price hikes are taken out of the calculation of y.o.y inflation and new, lower inflation rates are taken in, y.o.y inflation rates will decline. This decline will be particularly pronounced from August to November as the full blown effect of the food shock on inflation was felt last year during those particular months. The key risks to the current projection are: countryd5s risk premium movements, fiscal policy and food prices in the coming period. In recent days, concern has increased over the effects that may arise from the materialisation of risks in some advanced countries and currency zones. If the current crisis were to deepen, the risk premium could rise further, which may generate depreciation pressures with inflationary consequences. Unfavourable global developments could have negative repercussions on the Serbian economy. Together with falling prices of primary products worldwide, a drop in aggregate demand would have a disinflationary effect, which would partly alleviate the inflationary consequences of the rise in the countryd5s risk premium. As the latest crisis is a sovereign debt crisis, markets will be particularly sensitive to the pursuance of fiscal policy and any greater deviation from the planned budgetary framework could lead to a greater rise in risk premium and strengthening of depreciation pressures. In that sense, the Governmentd5s readiness, expressed at the recently held meeting with the National Bank, to keep fiscal policy within the agreed framework and to commence a new arrangement with the IMF, is of paramount importance for safeguarding macroeconomic stability. In regard to food prices, risks to the projection are present in both directions. If favourable weather conditions and a decline in world prices of primary agricultural products continue in the coming months, the disinflationary effects arising from food prices would be even more pronounced than assumed by our projection. Otherwise, bad weather in Serbia or in the countries of world major agricultural producers could trigger a rise in these prices. Given the favourable weather forecast, the latter scenario seems increasingly less probable, and it is our estimate that risks stemming from food prices would be rather disinflationary. In the coming period, we expect moderate economic recovery d0 GDP growth of 3% in 2011 and 4.5% in 2012. In the second half of 2011, a high contribution to growth will come from agricultural production. The initial indicators of this yeard5s agricultural yields are exceptionally encouraging, reflecting favourable weather conditions. In line with the usual seasonal cycle, growth in agricultural production is likely to be the strongest in the third quarter. On the expenditure side, the largest contribution to GDP growth is likely to come from rising investment activity. Though positive, the contribution of household consumption will be modest due to high unemployment and modest wage growth. Though smaller than in two previous years, the contribution of net exports will remain positive, mainly due to imports of equipment and intermediate goods spurred by the expected growth in investment activity. The most recent turmoil in global financial markets heightens the uncertainty as to the speed of economic recovery in the coming period, both worldwide and at home. We do not expect the global economy to decline as it did in 2009, yet the risks emanating from a possible downturn in global demand and deceleration in Serbiad5s economic growth still exist. Based on the current projection and its underlying risks, the Executive Board of the National Bank of Serbia views that the future path of the key policy rate will depend on the effects which may arise from the materialisation of risks in some advanced countries and currency zones, as well as possible fiscal risks at home. Should the fiscal policy remain within the agreed framework, as announced, there will be scope for further relaxation of monetary policy. The National Bank will closely monitor the developments in the international environment and the implementation of the planned budget framework, and will take appropriate measures based on estimated effects on the Serbian economy.

Title: Speech at the Presentation of the August Inflation Report
text: NATIONAL BANK OF SERBIA Speech at the Presentation of the August Inflation Report Belgrade, 15 August 2012 Ladies and gentlemen, esteemed members of the press and fellow economists, The factors fuelling inflationary pressures and at the same time dampening Serbiad5s economic growth include: uncertainty in the euro area and overall weaker global growth prospects, increased expansiveness of our fiscal policy since the start of the year, higher country risk premium and a downgrade of Serbiad5s credit rating, as well as unfavourable trends in global and domestic agricultural production. The main task ahead of the new government is the adoption of measures which would bring budget deficit and public debt in the medium term within the bounds envisaged by fiscal rules. The National Bank of Serbia expresses hope that the announced measures will be adopted to that effect, and that the agreement with the International Monetary Fund will, as a result, be renewed. This would send a positive signal to investors and contribute to improved risk perception, stabilisation of the foreign exchange market and weakening of inflationary pressures. The factors that played a key role in the rise of the country risk premium and the build-up of depreciation pressures this year were increased government spending, suspension of the arrangement with the International Monetary Fund and uncertainty in the euro area. And though the National Bank of Serbiad5s measures managed to appease the local foreign exchange market over the past several months, a more durable market stabilisation remains contingent on the adoption of credible fiscal measures and implementation of structural reforms. Bad weather conditions prompted a downward revision of agricultural production forecast for leading agricultural exporters since mid-June. Both worldwide and at home this precipitated a rise in the prices of primary commodities, such as wheat, corn and soybean, and renewed the cost push pressure on food prices. * * * As anticipated in earlier editions of the Inflation Report, inflation has been rising since May. At 6.1% in July, it passed the upper bound of the target tolerance band. Inflation was driven mainly by heightened cost-push pressures on food prices and rising import prices. Unprocessed food prices recorded the strongest upturn over the past few months, with fruit and vegetable prices rising on the back of droughty weather and the low base effect, and fresh meat prices going up on account of rising prices of fodder. Further inflationary pressures, primarily on import product prices, came from the weakening of the dinar. Year-on-year inflation is expected to continue rising in the period ahead. After peaking in the first half of 2013, it is expected to settle within the bounds of the target tolerance band by the end of the year. Inflation growth will be fuelled by several factors. Most notably, a surge in prices of primary agricultural commodities is expected to induce an increase in processed food prices. The high share of food in the consumer price index makes inflation highly sensitive to food price shocks, as shown by developments in the second half of 2010. Although the dinar may strengthen following the adoption of fiscal consolidation measures, past depreciation is likely to feed through to rising import product prices for some time yet. Growth in administered prices is also likely to pick up, as these prices were broadly flat in the year so far. Conversely, given rising unemployment and a modest outlook for economic growth both at home and abroad, low aggregate demand will continue to dampen price growth. * * * Economic activity increased by 0.6% from the previous quarter, but fell by 0.6% from the same period last year. The quarterly increase resulted in part from the low base effect of the first quarter of the year due to the extremely cold month of February. Faster growth in exports relative to imports and rising government consumption and investment gave a positive boost to economic growth in the second quarter, while domestic private demand, both investment and household, subsided. Drought-induced contraction in agricultural production and deterioration of the growth prospects of the euro area led to downward revisions of Serbiad5s GDP growth forecasts, from 0.5% to -0.5% for 2012, and from 3.0% to 2.5% for 2013. The prolonged drought is likely to significantly affect this yeard5s crop yields, primarily of corn, our main agricultural product. Bearing in mind the share of agricultural production in gross domestic product and exports, this will bear down considerably on economic activity and trade in the coming period. In addition, the downgrading of the next yeard5s growth forecasts for the euro area will reflect negatively on investment activity in Serbia and demand for our export products. On the other hand, exports will benefit from a production boost in the almost exclusively export-oriented automotive industry, and from the past weakening of the dinar. A further rise in the unemployment rate, which reached 25.5% in April, and a meagre increase in the household real income will continue to weigh on personal consumption and imports of consumer goods for some time yet. * * * In a bid to ease rising inflationary pressures, the National Bank of Serbia raised its key policy rate three times since June to the current level of 10.5%, while deciding at the same time to increase the portion of the required reserve allocations in dinars in order to withdraw dinar and free up foreign currency liquidity of banks. The monetary policy stance in the coming period will depend largely on the character of fiscal policy. Providing more efficient fiscal consolidation and structural reforms, including the continuation of the arrangement with the International Monetary Fund, price and financial stability can be delivered at a lower degree of monetary policy restrictiveness. The future path of the key policy rate will also depend on movements in food prices and their impact on year-ahead inflation expectations. To a degree, risks are also associated with future developments in the international environment. High sensitivity of financial markets in the current environment to any disruption in macroeconomic and financial stability should also be borne in mind. In this context, the best way for the government and the central bank to contribute to the improvement of the business environment is to pursue a policy which ensures long-term macroeconomic stability. Such policy implies a sustainable level of public debt, medium-term price stability, and a stable and resilient financial system. Stimulating the economy in a manner which is not sustainable over the long run would jeopardise the achievement of the above objectives and result in deepening of the foreign trade deficit, a rise in the country risk premium and costs of borrowing, and deterioration of the business and investment environment. Allow us to highlight once again that medium-term sustainability is more important than the pace of short-term economic growth. Consistent with the above, we express our expectation that fiscal consolidation measures to be taken in the immediate future will bring budget deficit and public debt in the medium term within the bounds envisaged by fiscal rules. On its part, the National Bank of Serbia will continue in the direction of stabilising medium-term inflation at a low level and maintaining a sound financial system, which in our opinion is the best way to support the economy in the current circumstances.

Title: Speech at the Presentation of the November Inflation Report
text: NATIONAL BANK OF SERBIA Speech at the presentation of the November Inflation Report Belgrade, 19 November 2012 Ladies and gentlemen, esteemed members of the press and fellow economists, The current year has been marked by high inflation and a fall in economic activity. Unfavourable economic developments are attributable to bad weather, growth in global food prices, fiscal expansion in the first half of the year, and slower economic recovery in Serbiad5s key trading partners. We expect the situation will improve next year both in terms of price and general macroeconomic stability and in terms of economic growth. * * * The current macroeconomic indicators for the euro area are not favourable either, and the 2013 forecasts for its growth and growth worldwide are lower than several months ago. On the other hand, international financial markets are calming down in response to the ECB and Fedd5s accommodative monetary policy measures, announced purchases of sovereign bonds and steps towards unified banking supervision in euro area member states. The announced fiscal consolidation at home and buoyed liquidity in the international financial market have bolstered investor interest in Serbia and pushed down the yields on Serbiad5s eurobonds. This indicates that the country risk premium is falling despite the August downgrade in Serbiad5s credit rating. Restrictive monetary policy measures and subsidised lending to the corporate sector, together with the mentioned fall in the country risk premium, have been the key factors behind the strengthening of the dinar over the past two months. Looking ahead, the perception of foreign investors will continue to depend most notably on the credibility of fiscal policy and sustainability of public debt. The National Bank of Serbia holds that the fiscal consolidation measures are a step in the right direction and expects that they will be supported by an agreement with the International Monetary Fund. This would send a positive signal to foreign investors, ease uncertainties surrounding the outlook for macroeconomic policy, and contribute to further lowering of the country risk premium. * * * Based on available data on expected yields, the National Bank of Serbia estimates that this yeard5s agricultural production will be lower by around one fifth than last year, which is triple the decline recorded in the drought years of 2003 and 2007. The actual downturn being significantly steeper relative to our expectations stated in the August Inflation Report, we have revised our GDP growth projection for 2012 from -0.5% down to -2.0%. At the same time, given the low base this year, the outturn for agricultural production next year is likely to be much higher. This explains why we have kept our GDP growth projection for 2013 at 2.5% despite the cutback in global growth forecasts. On the expenditure side, the economic contraction in 2012 is due to the drop in domestic private demand, consumption and investment alike. By contrast, government consumption, chiefly in the first half of the year, will provide a positive contribution. Even though this spurred imports in that period, and the poor agricultural yield and weak conjuncture in the international environment are affecting our exports, the contribution of net exports this year is likely to be positive, owing to the export of automobiles and the past weakening of the dinar. Consistent with the fiscal consolidation measures, we expect a fall in government consumption in 2013, while the high unemployment rate and the anticipated drop in real household income will have a dampening effect on private consumption too. On the other hand, a significant contribution to economic growth next year will come from export-oriented branches of the economy, the automobile industry in particular. Despite the fall in domestic consumption, we expect a modest growth in imports next year, driven by imports of intermediate goods for the needs of automobile industry and imports of equipment for investment purposes. * * * After rising for six months, inflation reached 12.9% in October. The growth in prices, notably those of food, was particularly pronounced in the last two months, which was expected given the long-lasting drought and the rising prices of production inputs. However, the intensity of these price hikes, which was more robust compared to both our expectations and the increase across the region, poses the question of adequacy of competition protection policy, commodity reserves policy and agrarian policy. The one-off increase in a large number of products, making up two thirds of the consumer price index basket, was also driven by the October increase in VAT from 18% to 20% and the extraordinary increase in excises on cigarettes and petroleum products. After being flat for one year, administered prices were raised in October (public transportation and utilities services) in some towns. Inflationary pressures were further fuelled by the lagged effects of past depreciation of the dinar. Nevertheless, we estimate that the inflationary shock is behind us and that monthly inflation rates will slow down starting from November, while a rise in year-on-year inflation, due to the low base, will continue in the months to come. We expect year-on-year inflation to decline as of the second quarter of 2013 and to return within the target tolerance band by the end of 2013. Food prices will continue to rise for some time yet. However, with the coming of the new agricultural season and the expected lowering of prices of primary agricultural commodities as of the second quarter of 2013, food prices will contribute to a drop in year-on-year inflation. Fruit and vegetable prices will be the first to drag down inflation, particularly in May and June, while the lowering of prices of primary agricultural commodities, such as wheat and corn, will have a gradual effect through falling costs in the production of processed food. The effects of the past depreciation of the dinar have been almost fully exhausted and we expect no further inflationary pressures from this source. Price growth will also slow down largely on account of the exceptionally low aggregate demand caused by plummeting real household income and a high unemployment rate. On the other hand, the months to come are likely to see a rise in some administered prices, which will compensate for the lack of their adjustment in the past period. * * * Ladies and gentlemen, in view of the supply-side shocks, such as the agricultural shock and VAT increase, monetary policy of the National Bank of Serbia aims to mitigate the spill-over of the resulting price growth to other prices through rising inflation expectations. This is the main rationale behind our restrictive measures, i.e. raises in the key policy rate, from 9.5% to 10.95%, and the increase in the dinar share of allocations under foreign exchange required reserves. Measures of the National Bank of Serbia will continue to focus on bringing inflation back within the target tolerance band of 4b11.5%. In our opinion, measures of the central bank towards preserving medium-term price and financial stability, and the Governmentd5s measures aimed at public finance consolidation, are the best way to help the economy in the current circumstances as they will lower the countryd5s risk and borrowing costs, and make the business and investment conditions more stable.

Title: Speech at the Presentation of the February Inflation Report
text: NATIONAL BANK OF SERBIA Speech at Presentation of February 2013 Inflation Report Belgrade, 13 February 2013 Late 2012 was characterised by the weakening of inflationary pressures and moderate growth of economy, including narrowing of the foreign trade deficit. We expect such movements to continue in the current year. According to our projections, after measuring 12.2% in December, inflation will return within the target tolerance band by the end of 2013, while the economic activity, after declining by around 2% in 2012, will grow by around 2.5% in 2013. * ** In contrast to Serbia and according to estimates, the euro area economy will remain in recession. Following a 0.4% drop in 2012, GDP in the euro area is expected to contract by 0.1% to 0.2% this year. Despite unfavourable tendencies in the real sector, financial markets are recovering and yields on sovereign bonds of the euro area periphery are declining. This is due to European Central Bankd5s sovereign debt purchase programme, steps towards tighter fiscal integration and the agreement on These measures, together with further monetary policy easing in the leading world economies, contributed strongly to falling yields on Serbiad5s eurobonds, i.e. to a decline in the countryd5s risk premium over the past five months. Risk premia across the region began to decline in July after the European Central Bankd5s governor pledged to do d2whatever it takesd3 to save the euro. The fall in Serbiad5s risk premium began a few months later, after the announcement of fiscal consolidation measures. Increased monetary policy restrictiveness, fiscal consolidation measures and falling risk premium were the key factors behind the dinard5s appreciation since September. This meant the reversal of the depreciation trend from the first eight months of 2012. Such developments in the foreign exchange market were also driven by elevated foreign currency sales following the extension of subsidised loans. * * * In the last quarter of 2012, the economy grew 0.3% relative to the previous quarter, but was 1.5% down on the same period of 2011. At the year-level, GDP declined by around 2%, chiefly as a result of the drought-induced agricultural downturn at home and recession in the euro area. The last quarter saw a 2.1% recovery of industrial production, mainly due to increased production in automobile and oil industries. As the automobile industry is almost fully export-oriented, Serbiad5s GDP growth on the expenditure side in the fourth quarter was largely generated by net exports. Government consumption provided a positive contribution to growth. On the other hand, domestic private demand, both consumption and investment, declined. In the current year, agricultural recovery and expansion of automobile and oil industries will be the key generators of economic growth of around 2.5%. Consistent with this, net exports will give the main impetus to GDP growth despite the modest outlook for recovery of our key foreign trade partners. Furthermore, a positive contribution is likely to come from private investment which was exceptionally low in 2012. On the other hand, fiscal consolidation measures are expected to diminish government consumption, while private consumption is likely to fall owing to declining real household income. * * * Growth in year-on-year inflation slowed down during the fourth quarter, arriving at 12.2% in December. Inflationary pressures were most pronounced in October, driven not only by higher costs of food production inputs and the effects of past weakening of the dinar, but also by the increase in However, after a 2.8% monthly rise in October, consumer prices stagnated in November, only to decline by 0.4% in December. Such movements in the last two months of 2012 resulted from lower prices of certain food products mainly on account of dampened demand, caused by considerable price hikes in the prior period. We expect year-on-year inflation to return within the target tolerance band (4b11.5%) by the end of the current year. It will, however, keep rising for another several months on account of the expected increase in administered prices and the low base effect. In the year to date, an increase has been recorded for prices of cigarettes (due to excise tax harmonisation), medicaments and natural gas. Higher electricity prices are also quite likely in the coming months. As of the second quarter, however, with the onset of the new agricultural season and a decrease in prices of agricultural commodities, year-on-year inflation is likely to decline. Fruit and vegetable prices will be the first to directly impact a decline in inflation (most notably in May and June), while cheaper primary agricultural commodities, such as wheat and corn, will exert a more gradual effect The past strengthening of the dinar, feeding through to lower import prices, should make a significant downward pressure on inflation in 2013. Low aggregate demand is also likely to work in the same, disinflationary direction, given the still high unemployment and low real income of households. Declining inflation expectations and consistent implementation of fiscal consolidation measures will also ease the upward pressure on prices. * * * Responding to rising inflationary pressures, the National Bank of Serbia tightened its monetary policy stance over the last eight months. In this period, the key policy rate was raised from 9.5% to 11.75%, dinar allocations under foreign exchange reserve requirements were increased, while the direction of main operations was reversed in December, to mop up excess dinar liquidity. Full-blown effects on inflation will be seen in the course of this year. With the waning of the inflationary shock caused by food and administered prices, the National Bank of Serbiad5s Executive Board will consider the possibility of easing its monetary policy stance in the coming months. However, as unexpected changes in the impact of some factors on the above inflation projection remain possible, the expectations with regard to the character of monetary policy in the coming period are in no way binding on the National Bank of Serbia. * * * Ladies and gentlemen, the National Bank of Serbiad5s actions towards maintaining medium term price and financial stability and the implementation of the Governmentd5s public finance consolidation measures are the best way to help the economy in the long run. At the same time, this will push down the country risk and borrowing costs, while enabling a more stable business and investment environment, which is confirmed by the movements observed over the last several months.

Title: Speech at the Presentation of the May 2013 Inflation Report
text: NATIONAL BANK OF SERBIA Speech at the presentation of the Inflation Report May 2013 Belgrade, 22 May 2013 Ladies and gentlemen, esteemed members of the press and fellow economists, Receding inflationary pressures and moderate economic growth marked the beginning of 2013. We expect such tendencies to continue and to result in the return of year-on-year inflation within the target tolerance band by October, and economic growth of around 2% this year. * * * The economic downturn in the euro area continued in early 2013 and the projected start of economic recovery has been shifted to the second half of the year. The downturn for the entire 2013 is expected at around 0.3d00.4%. On the other hand, despite occasional turbulences, such as the one triggered by the Cypriot financial crisis in March, the tendency of easing the financial strain in the euro area still persists. Lower risk aversion in the global financial market, together with economic policy measures in Serbia, brought about a vigorous decline in the country risk premium since September last year. EMBI, a risk premium indicator, currently stands at around 330 basis points, down by around 270 basis points from August last year. Following the period of relative stability in the first quarter of 2013, new appreciation pressures ensued, fuelled by the European Commissiond5s recommendation on the start of negotiations on Serbiad5s accession to the European Union. To ease these pressures, The National Bank of Serbia engaged in purchasing foreign currency in the interbank foreign exchange market. Fiscal consolidation is crucial to the maintenance of macroeconomic stability. As it is already certain that this yeard5s planned budget deficit of 3.6% of GDP will be exceeded, new fiscal consolidation measures should be implemented to ensure long-term sustainability of public debt. A new precautionary arrangement with the IMF would serve as additional support to macroeconomic stability and a trigger for a more positive perception of Serbia. * * * According to preliminary estimates, in the first three months of 2013 economic growth was 1.9% year-on-year, or 1.5% quarter-on-quarter. Economic growth has so far been almost fully generated by net exports, while domestic demand remains stagnant. A rise in exports over the last two quarters was driven primarily by automobile exports, which is also the main reason behind the narrowing of the current account deficit in this period. At the level of entire 2013, we have revised our earlier growth forecast of 2.5% down to around 2.0%, chiefly on account of deteriorated outlook for economic recovery in the euro area and our other foreign trade partners. Though both domestic and global demand will be low this year, we expect the economic activity to grow on account of recovery of agricultural production and the improved capacity utilisation in automobile and oil industries. These two sectors will in fact lend the key boost to exports in the coming period. Together with fiscal consolidation measures, this is likely to narrow the current account deficit in 2013 by around 2 percentage points of GDP relative to the previous year. * * * Inflationary pressures further abated in early 2013. Though year-on-year inflation was still high in April d0 it reached 11.4%, monthly inflation rates over the last six months averaged 0.25%, which is consistent with the inflation target level (4b11.5%). A slowdown in inflation began in late 2012, first on account of food prices, and continued this year based on unprocessed food prices. The growth of inflation excluding food and energy, the so-called core inflation, also slowed down in the year to date, averaging 0.25%. A similar increase was recorded in processed food prices, while the prices of unprocessed food, notably vegetables, registered a stronger seasonal rise. As for administered prices, there was an upswing in the prices of medicaments and natural gas, as well as of cigarettes, driven by excise adjustments. Relatively high monthly inflation in April of 0.8% was mostly attributable to a hike in the prices of several types of vegetables and will not affect the pace of the inflationd5s return within the target tolerance band. In the coming period, we expect year-on-year inflation to fall and settle within the bounds of the target tolerance band by October. The key contribution to its drop will come from lower prices of primary commodities, stable foreign exchange rate and low aggregate demand. Over the past months, the prices of primary agricultural commodities fell both in the international and domestic markets d0 by 20% in all, relative to last yeard5s August peak. Market expectations indicate that the drop will continue in the period ahead given the favourable forecasts regarding this yeard5s global agricultural yields. Such developments will lead to a further decrease in the costs of food production, whose effects this year will be disinflationary. In addition, we expect to see a drop in fruit and vegetable prices as they are still relatively high following the drought in 2012. As for primary commodities, world oil prices have also receded by around 7% since early 2013, bringing down the prices of derivatives and opening a possibility of their further decrease. Additionally, the drop in the country risk premium and moderate strengthening of the dinar in the previous period induced a fall in import product prices, which has already helped decelerate the pace of monthly inflation. We expect that the disinflationary effect of the foreign exchange rate will continue in the foreseeable future. Despite the projected GDP growth, persistent exceptionally low aggregate demand will act in the same direction. Allow me to reiterate that this yeard5s economic growth will not be driven by higher demand, but by increased utilisation of capacities in the automobile and oil industries, as well as a recovery in agricultural production. Over the coming period, the decline in year-on-year inflation should continue hand in hand with decreasing inflationary expectations, which will additionally spur the disinflation process. Administered prices will be the only ones with an inflationary effect in the near future, primarily on account of the announced upturn in the price of electricity. This will only slow the fall in inflation, but will not jeopardize its return within the target tolerance band. Year-on-year inflation figures will also be declining on account of the high base effect, as last yeard5s hikes, that were particularly strong in the period Mayd0October 2012, will be gradually phased out from the calculations. * * * Having assessed that inflationary pressures are falling and that the return of inflation within the bounds of the target tolerance band is certain d0 the National Bank of Serbia decided last week to trim the key policy rate from 11.75% down to 11.25%. Given the receding inflationary pressures, the Executive Board of the National Bank of Serbia will consider the possibility of further monetary policy easing in the coming period. However, as unexpected changes in the impact of some factors on the above inflation projection remain possible, the expectation stated with regard to the character of monetary policy in the period ahead is in no way binding on the NBS. The Executive Board estimates that monetary policy measures will be significantly affected by international developments, fiscal movements and the effect of the new agricultural season on food prices. In any case, all National Bank of Serbiad5s measures will be aimed at maintaining price and financial stability.

Title: Speech at the Presentation of the August 2013 Inflation Report
text: NATIONAL BANK OF SERBIA Speech at the presentation of the Inflation Report August 2013 Belgrade, 14 August 2013 Ladies and gentlemen, esteemed members of the press and fellow economists, It is a pleasure for me to present the August Inflation Report of the National Bank of Serbia and our view of current economic developments and their outlook in the period ahead. Inflationary pressures have weakened further since we last met in May, and economic activity indicators seem to suggest ever more clearly that the recovery begun in the last quarter of 2012 is taking hold. As we have already announced, we expect year-on-year inflation to fall back within the target tolerance band by October and to stay within the band thereafter. You will notice that our new inflation projection is almost the same as the one released in May. The new projection of GDP growth in 2013 also remains unchanged at around 2.0%. The projection of GDP growth in 2014, however, has been revised down from 3.0% to around 2.5% as the growth prospects for Serbiad5s main foreign trade partners deteriorated in the meantime. Still, the expected growth of our economy remains above the average of its South East European peers. The economic recovery is undeniably slower than we would all like it to be, but given the intensity and the scale of the crisis, it is quite clear that the recovery cannot be swift and without difficulties. The good news is that it is becoming increasingly evident that the domestic economic activity is on the path of sustainable growth and that external imbalance is narrowing. * * * Growth projections for the euro area have been revised down d0 according to the European Central Bank, the International Monetary Fund and Consensus Forecast, the euro area economy will contract by 0.6% in 2013. Still, an improvement in the early economic activity indicators in the last two months heralds an end to the recession. Particularly encouraging is the slowing pace of contraction of highly-indebted euro area members. The ECB reduced its main refinancing rate in May to the historical low of 0.5%. The Fed, by contrast, suggested that it might taper its quantitative easing through 2013 and wind it down altogether around mid-2014 if economic growth becomes firm enough. The Fedd5s hint gave rise to instability in the international financial markets as investors reacted by reducing their exposure towards riskier markets. The yields on sovereign bonds rose, country risk premiums increased and the currencies of nearly all countries in the region depreciated. In the case of Serbia, this effect was further amplified by the IMFd5s statement on the necessity of taking additional fiscal consolidation measures. Similarly to other central banks, the NBS intervened during this period by selling foreign exchange in the foreign exchange market. The situation in the international financial markets gradually eased in the course of July. EMBI for Serbia fell from the June high and the dinar edged up slightly against the euro. Besides, Fitch affirmed Serbiad5s credit rating, ending speculations of a possible downgrade which emerged after Moodyd5s assigned to Serbia a comparatively one notch lower rating. * * * * * * External imbalance narrowed in 2013 faster than we expected d0 in the first six months, the current account deficit was by 53.5% lower compared to the same period last year, and equalled 5.7% of estimated GDP. Rather more important is the fact that a reduction in the current account deficit originates primarily from the significant increase in exports relative to imports (20% vs. 2% year-on.year). Positive changes in terms of narrowing of external imbalance are also corroborated by increased exports not only in the motor vehicles category, but also in other sectors (the chemical industry, production of rubber and plastic products, electrical equipment etc). The start-up of investments primarily in automobile and oil industries, and fiscal consolidation, are expected to bring down the share of the current account deficit in GDP from 10.5% in 2012 to below 7.0% this year. This share should continue to decline over the coming years. GDP growth in 2013 and 2014 will be led mainly by rising net exports and to a lesser extent by private investments. According to our estimate, private consumption will decline this year because of lower real income and sluggish growth in lending activity, while the contraction in government consumption will be due to the implementation of fiscal consolidation measures. The deviation from the projection is equally possible in either direction and depends primarily on the speed of economic recovery of Serbiad5s main foreign trade partners and the outcome of this yeard5s agricultural season. * * * Year-on-year inflation moved in Q2 in accordance with expectations presented in the May Inflation Report. Inflation continued down and reached 8.6% in July. However, the year-on-year inflation rate still remains relatively high, but this is due mainly to price growth recorded from August to October 2012. Of the mentioned 8.6%, as much as 6.9 percentage points relates to price growth in that period. In other words, the average monthly inflation rate from November last year to July this year was 0.2%. Inflation declined as a result of past restrictive monetary policy measures, a reduction in raw material costs in food production, low aggregate demand and relative stability of the exchange rate. According to our estimates, with the exclusion of high last yeard5s price growth from calculation, year.on-year inflation will accelerate down in the third quarter. The key disinflationary factor in the coming period will be lower food production costs, expected mainly on account of a further reduction in prices of primary agricultural commodities. It is quite certain already that this yeard5s agricultural season will be much better than the last one both at home and abroad. In view of this, raw material costs in domestic food production are expected to be lower at least until the next agricultural season, and so are the rates of food inflation. On the other hand, administered prices will rise this year by around 10% and will contribute 2.0 percentage points to inflation, mainly because of the electricity price increase. As we have emphasised several times already, this will not jeopardise the return of inflation within the target tolerance band. Also, the weakening of the dinar in late May and in June may send upward pressure on import prices, but the intensity of this pressure will depend on the importersd5 ability to increase prices against the backdrop of depressed demand. Given all of the above, we expect that inflation will return within the target tolerance band by October and stay within the band thereafter. Let us recall, the National Bank of Serbiad5s inflation target is 4 b1 1.5%. * * * Guided by the analysis of current and expected macroeconomic developments, the Executive Board of the National Bank of Serbia decided last week to keep the key policy rate at 11.0%. Assuming agricultural commodity prices decline further, no external shocks occur and fiscal consolidation is implemented as planned, the Executive Board will consider further monetary policy easing in the coming period. It is indisputable that our economy is slowly recovering. However, in order to ensure sustainable economic growth and keep inflation within the target tolerance band, additional efforts are needed towards a further reduction in internal and external imbalances. An important step to this effect is the adoption of the revised budget and new measures of structural adjustment, which is why the National Bank of Serbia supports the Governmentd5s commitment to implementing the announced measures. Consistent implementation of these measures would improve investor perception of Serbia and create the leeway for further monetary policy easing.

Title: Speech at the Presentation of the November 2013 Inflation Report
text: NATIONAL BANK OF SERBIA Speech at the presentation of the Inflation Report d0 November 2013 Branko Hini., General Manager of the Directorate for Economic Research and Statistics Belgrade, 19 November 2013 Ladies and gentlemen, esteemed members of the press and fellow economists, Since we last met at the presentation of the August Report, inflationary pressures have receded further and economic recovery has moved along. As announced repeatedly by the National Bank of Serbia over the last year and a half, year-on-year inflation has returned within the target tolerance band in September. Even though it undershot the target in October when it fell to 2.2%, year-on-year inflation is expected to move within the target tolerance band in the coming period. The new inflation projection is lower than the one released in August mainly owing to the very good agricultural season whose effects reflected on food prices more than anticipated earlier. While the projection of GDP growth in 2013 remains unchanged at around 2%, the projection for 2014 has been revised down to around 1.5% on account of the dampening effects that fiscal consolidation measures are likely to produce on consumption in the near term. These measures, however, must be implemented in order to ensure public finance sustainability and macroeconomic stability which are the key prerequisites for viable economic growth. The reduction of external imbalance has proceeded at an even faster pace than expected earlier. As a result, the current account deficit of the balance of payments is projected to contract to around 4d0 5% of GDP this year. * * * The global economic environment remained in the third quarter under the dominant sway of developments in the United States, i.e. anticipation of the Fedd5s decision on the monetary stimulus tapering and the budget and debt ceiling crises. Uncertainty in the international financial markets persisted until the Fedd5s September meeting which postponed the decision on the start of reduction of the quantitative easing programme. Coupled with positive foreign trade trends, this led to the weakening of depreciation pressures in the domestic market from mid-September onwards and paved the way for appreciation pressures in October. An additional impetus to appreciation pressures came from the announcement of fiscal consolidation measures, which encouraged non.residents to invest into government securities. In October and November the National Bank of Serbia intervened in the interbank foreign exchange market on the side of purchase. In the year to date, the National Bank sold EUR 425 million in the interbank foreign exchange market and bought EUR 365 million. By intervening in both directions, the National Bank has once again confirmed its commitment to preventing major short-term fluctuations, without targeting any specific level of the exchange rate. Market concerns and reactions to the Fedd5s monetary policy reflected on risk premium movements across the region. Our risk premium, measured by the Emerging Markets Bond Index (EMBI), followed the regional pattern, with somewhat more pronounced changes in both directions compared to other countries. Mid-November, Serbiad5s EMBI stood at 438 basis points. Though the euro area emerged from recession in the second quarter, it is still too early to speak of a major recovery, as the pace of growth remains uneven. Encouraging, though, is a much better outlook for the euro area economyd0 its fall in 2013 is likely to be smaller and its growth in 2014 stronger than expected before. The recovery of economic activity should also be aided by the lowering of the ECB rate to the historical low of 0.25% in November. * * * Domestic economy grew 1.1% seasonally-adjusted in the third quarter, led by a boost in industrial and agricultural production, as well as by net exports on the expenditure side. These factors will also determine the annual movements of GDP, which is estimated to go up by around 2%. We expect that the incipient euro area recovery and the beginning of Serbiad5s negotiations on EU membership will boost investment in 2014 and encourage a rise in net exports. Nevertheless, due to fiscal consolidation measures, the contribution of government and household consumption to growth will remain negative. Hence, GDP growth in 2014 has been projected at around 1.5%. The current account deficit in the three months to September stood at only 1.4% of estimated GDP. It decreased owing to continued expansion in the automobile industry in particular, the effect of substitution of petroleum products imports, higher inflow from remittances, and fiscal consolidation measures. For the first time, quarterly exports reached EUR 3 billion. Relative to the same period last year, exports in the third quarter rose by 38.2% and imports by 10.5%. The annual current account deficit is expected to be 4d05% of GDP, which is below expectations stated in the August Inflation Report. * * * Inflationary pressures have continued to ease. In the year to October, inflation reached 2.6%, of which 2.1 percentage points are attributable to growth of administered prices, while food prices recorded a decline. In line with expectations which the National Bank of Serbia has communicated during the past year and a half, year-on-year inflation returned within the target tolerance band in September. In addition to monetary policy measures, the push was also generated by the fall in primary agricultural products, low aggregate demand and relative stability of the dinar exchange rate. By October, core inflation also returned within the tolerance band (consumer prices excluding food, energy, alcohol beverages and cigarettes). Last yeard5s high base and the fall in food prices resulted in year-on-year inflation undershooting the target in October and reaching 2.2%. It is expected to rise gradually towards the target over the next two months and to fall within the tolerance band by the end of the year, though still short of 4%. To recall, the National Bank of Serbiad5s objective is to have inflation at 4 b1 1.5% by the end of 2016. A decline in year-on-year inflation was accompanied by subsiding inflation expectations of all sectors. Expectations of the financial sector have been within the target tolerance band since October. Falling inflation and inflation expectations have made dinar interest rates more attractive and boosted dinar savings. In October and the first half of November, dinar savings rose by RSD 5.7 billion. Since early 2013, they have grown by RSD 11.4 billion. According to our projection, inflation will move within the target tolerance band next year. The main disinflationary factors in the coming period will be very low costs in food production and low aggregate demand. The disinflationary effect of domestic demand will be further amplified by the Governmentd5s economic measures which will reflect on lower government and household consumption next year. On the other hand, the one-off direct effect of the VAT increase on inflation is estimated at 0.5 percentage points. The indirect effect will be small and limited by the producersd5 opportunity to raise prices against the background of low domestic demand. Risks to the inflation projection are associated chiefly with developments in the international environment and access to external finance against expected monetary policy easing of central banks of developed countries. Implementation of credible fiscal consolidation measures may ease possible negative effects in this regard. * * * Having analysed current and expected macroeconomic developments, the National Bank of Serbiad5s Executive Board decided at its last meeting to cut the key policy rate by 0.5 percentage points down to 10%. Given the subsiding of inflationary pressures and assuming fiscal consolidation is implemented as planned, the Executive Board will consider further monetary policy easing in the coming period. However, as unexpected changes in the impact of some factors on the inflation projection remain possible, the expectation with regard to the character of monetary policy in the coming period is in no way binding on the NBS. In view of the risks we are facing, a durable reduction in external imbalance is an imperative and requires improvement in the fiscal position. The National Bank of Serbia therefore supports the Governmentd5s commitment to consistent implementation of consolidation measures, which will ensure macroeconomic stability and open up additional scope for further monetary policy easing.

Title: Governors introductory address at the presentation of the Inflation Report  November 2013
text: NATIONAL BANK OF SERBIA Governord5s introductory address at the presentation of the Inflation Report d0 November 2013 Dr Jorgovanka Tabakovi., Governor Belgrade, 19 November 2013 Ladies and gentlemen, esteemed members of the press and fellow economists, Allow me to use this opportunity to thank you for the attention you are giving to the Inflation Report and our assessments of current economic developments and their prospects for the coming period. Let us first go back to what we had announced last year and discuss what happened in the meantime. A year ago the National Bank of Serbia said that inflation would return within the target tolerance band in the second half of 2013 and that the economic recovery would be accompanied by a decrease in external imbalance. In contrast, some analysts at the time were anticipating two-digit inflation by the end of 2013, as well as significant weakening of the dinar, excessive spending of foreign exchange reserves and continuing recession. Actual economic developments have clearly proved them wrong. But first things first, measuring 4.9% in September, year-on-year inflation has returned within the target tolerance band of 4b11.5%. This shows that the National Bank of Serbia has not only been right in its assessment of the nature of inflationary pressures, but that it also weighed policy action carefully and has ultimately taken measures that helped maintain price and financial stability, without any detriment to the nascent economic recovery. Inflation declined further in October. It now measures 2.2% and is temporarily below the lower bound of the target tolerance band. Given that inflation is already low, future monetary policy measures will be aimed at keeping it within the target. Consistency in monetary policy implementation and the results achieved so far have been acknowledged by the financial sector, businesses and households alike. This is illustrated by the fact that their one-year ahead inflation expectations have fallen considerably and trended closer to the target. We expect that our perseverance in maintaining low inflation will anchor inflation expectations to the target which has been set until the end of 2016 at 4%. Thanks to significantly improved foreign trade trends, the current account deficit has been more than halved relative to the previous year. This means that external imbalance is decreasing even faster than expected. It was owing to positive trends in external economic relations that the dinar has remained stable, despite changeable conditions in the international financial market and the perception of sustainability of domestic public finance. The National Bank of Serbia intervened in the interbank foreign exchange market in order to prevent both excessive daily strengthening and excessive daily weakening of the dinar. Economic growth, set in train in late 2012, continued this year. However, the recovery of our economy, and almost all other economies, is slower than expected. It was only this summer, nearly five years after the collapse of Lehman Brothers and the start of the global economic crisis of enormous magnitude, that developed countries showed signs of a possibly sustainable economic recovery. This is encouraging, but it also means that the time is drawing near when central banks of developed countries will start exiting the quantitative easing program, confronting Serbia and other emerging economies with new economic challenges. Still, I believe we can overcome these challenges and, through coordination of monetary and fiscal policies, ensure higher economic growth rates and lower unemployment. Higher productivity will trigger a rise in real incomes and purchasing power, leading to the recovery of domestic demand, i.e. real improvement of living conditions of our citizens. This is the result that we are striving for. At the same time, remaining committed to price and financial stability, we support the Government in the pursuit of its economic policy. Let me also comment on the results achieved during the recent d2Savings Weekd3. I was very pleased to see that banks were complying with the National Bank of Serbiad5s recommendation on the level of interest rates. Also, the practice of attracting savings deposits with high interest rates was almost fully abandoned. We are also satisfied with the fact that over the past year our citizens have been increasingly turning to saving in dinars and recognising its greater profitability compared to saving in foreign exchange. Finally, my hope and expectation is that low and stable inflation, as well as stable exchange rate, will make it possible for all of us to direct our attention to saving and the efficiency of investments which are of paramount importance for the sustainability of economic growth in future. Thank you for your attention.

Title: Speech at the closing ceremony and press conference on the completion of the IPA project Strengthening the Institutional Capacities of the National Bank of Serbia
text: NATIONAL BANK OF SERBIA Governord5s Introductory Statement at the closing ceremony and press conference on the completion of the IPA project d2Strengthening the Institutional Capacities of the National Bank of Serbiad3 PhD Jorgovanka Tabakovi., Governor Belgrade, 12 December 2013 Esteemed colleagues, members of the press, ladies and gentlemen It is my great honour and pleasure to bid you welcome to the National Bank of Serbia on the occasion of the successful conclusion of the IPA project d2Strengthening of the Institutional Capacities of the National Bank of Serbiad3. First of all, I would like to greet our dear guests, Mr J9arg Asmussen, member of the Executive Board of the European Central Bank and Mr Michael Davenport, Head of the European Union Delegation to the Republic of Serbia. I also extend my sincere greetings to the ambassadors of European Union countries, representatives of national central banks of the European System of Central Banks, as well as representatives of the Government of the Republic of Serbia. We have gathered here today to mark the successful conclusion of the project d2Strengthening of the Institutional Capacities of the National Bank of Serbiad3. The project was implemented in direct cooperation with the European Central Bank and was financed from the European Union.s Instrument for Pre-Accession Assistance d0 IPA. The project involved participation of representatives of the European Central Bank and experts from 21 central banks of EU countries, which makes this project one of the largest of its kind. The project aimed to align the operation of the National Bank of Serbia with best European practice and central banking standards implemented in the European System of Central Banks. Since 1 February 2011, when the project was launched, over 170 activities have been implemented in 13 areas of National Bank of Serbia.s operation. Deliverables include supervision manuals for banks, insurance companies and voluntary pension funds, as well as action plans to upgrade foreign exchange reserves management, statistics, financial stability, accounting and information technology. Important strategies were prepared in the field of liberalisation of capital movement, protection of financial services consumers, and the enhancement of efficiency in the money market. Furthermore, laws were drafted in the area of payment services to incorporate the EU.s regulatory framework. The project also enabled the development of econometric models to strengthen the National Bank of Serbia.s research function. Besides, it helped improve capacities for harmonisation of domestic regulations with EU legislation and enhance European integration activities. It is my great pleasure to say that project objectives have been successfully achieved. Moreover, the implementation of deliverables is particularly important for the oncoming negotiations of the Republic of Serbia with the European Union, in which our institution will play a highly active role. Besides appointing its representatives in the most important negotiation bodies, the National Bank of Serbia has reaffirmed its commitment to the negotiation process and will be leading negotiations in chapters e3financial services. and e3economic and monetary policy.. The National Bank of Serbia has also assumed an important role in the field of e3free movement of capital.. We have gained tremendously from cooperating with colleagues from EU central banks who have helped us to better prepare ourselves for future challenges. Let me extend my special gratitude to the European Union Delegation to the Republic of Serbia and the European Commission whose financial support made this project happen. I would also like to highlight the exceptional work of our dear colleagues from the European Central Bank.s project team, led by Mr Michael Olsen. I also warmly thank the experts of European Union central banks who contributed to the achievement of project deliverables. Employees of the National Bank of Serbia had a unique opportunity to learn, exchange experiences and make contacts with colleagues from a number of central banks. To conclude, there is no doubt that projects such as this one enable communication with European partners and finding of solutions which serve our best interest, and we plan to continue to participate in similar projects and cooperate with our colleagues from the European Union. I am quite confident that this IPA project marks only the beginning of a successful cooperation which will continue in the years to come. Thank you very much for your attention.

Title: Speech at the Presentation of the February 2014 Inflation Report
text: NATIONAL BANK OF SERBIA Speech at the presentation of the Inflation Report d0 February 2014 Branko Hini., General Manager of the Directorate for Economic Research and Statistics Belgrade, 20 February 2014 Ladies and gentlemen, esteemed members of the press and fellow economists, Positive tendencies highlighted in the previous issues of the Inflation Report have continued d0 inflation is running low, and economic growth, led by net exports, has exceeded our expectations for 2013. The surprisingly steep fall in prices of unprocessed food, notably fruit, has pushed y-o-y inflation in Q4 2013 below the lower bound of the target tolerance band. We expect that y-o-y inflation will return within the target tolerance band of 4b11.5% in the course of this quarter and that it will stay within the band thereafter. As agricultural production performed much better than anticipated, GDP growth in 2013 amounted to 2.4%, thereby exceeding the expected 2.0%. It is precisely because of the higher last yeard5s base for agricultural production that we have trimmed down our growth forecast for this year. According to the new projection, GDP should grow by around 1.0% in 2014 and by around 2.00% in 2015. * * * In the period under review, the international environment was again marked by the monetary policy moves of the Fed. As the US economy stepped up its growth and signals from the labour market improved, as of January the Fed started to wind down its quantitative easing programme. Along the lines of what happened last summer, investors worldwide reacted by exiting the riskier assets of emerging market economies, principally those running huge current account deficits, and in doing so sent depreciation pressures on the local currencies. In addition to intervening in the foreign exchange market, several central banks responded to these pressures also by raising their policy rates. Our foreign exchange market has not escaped the far-reaching impact of the Fedd5s decisions either. Namely, appreciation pressures in Q4 were, inter alia, attributable to the fall in the country risk premium and increased non-resident interest in dinar securities after the Fed delayed the decision on tapering its monetary stimulus in September. Appreciation pressures were also aided by a somewhat larger inflow of FDI, relatively favourable foreign trade movements and adoption of a new set of fiscal consolidation measures. The main reasons behind depreciation pressures since the beginning of the year are the start of the Fedd5s tapering and stronger FX demand of domestic enterprises, notably energy importers. Buying foreign exchange in late 2013 and selling it since the start of the year, the National Bank of Serbia has remained consistent in its policy of intervening in order to ease excessive short-term volatility of the exchange rate. Looking ahead, the main uncertainties in the external environment are associated with the reaction of financial markets to the Fedd5s tapering of asset purchases, as this will determine the intensity of the effect on emerging market currencies. Closer to home, the economic outlook for the euro area in 2014 is now slightly brighter. After contracting in 2012 and 2013, the euro area economy is expected to grow by 1.0% this year. Gradual recovery of demand in the currency bloc should have a positive impact on Serbiad5s economy and foreign trade. In response to deflationary pressures, the ECB has cut its policy rate to 0.25% and hinted at additional monetary easing depending on how the situation in the economy evolves. * * * Exports declined in Q4, mirroring lower automobile industry output. Together with a mild rise in imports, this led to a quarterly decline in GDP by 0.5% s-a. Still, looking at the year as a whole, foreign trade flows were much more favourable than in the previous years, which reflected positively on movements in the foreign exchange market. Exports were led chiefly by the automobile industry, but most other branches of manufacturing also recorded a rise in exports. While expansion of the export base represents a positive signal, further reduction of the foreign trade deficit requires new investment into export-oriented sectors. In Q4, domestic demand of the private sector recorded growth on the back of higher investment in current assets, and was also bolstered by a mild rise in consumption, mirrored primarily through growth in retail trade. By contrast, government consumption and investment were on the decline. GDP growth is likely to slow to around 1.0% this year. The forecast is based on assumptions of an average agricultural season and the waning effects of the automobile and oil industries. On the demand-side it is grounded in the expected fall in final consumption, slight recovery of investments and rising demand of our main trade partners. On the expenditure side, growth should be driven by net exports, as recovery is anticipated in the euro area. Another factor propelling investments up will be the formal opening of Serbiad5s EU accession negotiations, as well as last yeard5s low base. Household and government consumption will exert a negative effect on growth, mostly because of the upcoming fiscal adjustment measures. Nevertheless, fiscal consolidation and the announced structural reforms will create room for GDP growth to pick up in the coming years, which should be additionally aided by further recovery in the euro area. * * * Inflationary pressures in 2013 stayed rather low, especially in the second half of the year when the average monthly inflation was negative (-0.1%). Administered prices gave a significant push to price growth in 2013, while low aggregate demand and reduced food production costs acted as the main disinflationary factors. Low domestic demand will remain the key disinflationary factor in the period ahead, while inflation will be driven up by the rise in administered prices, coupled with a one-time pass-through effect of the special VAT rate increase. With the onset of a new agricultural season, which we assume will be average, the prices of fruit, vegetables and primary agricultural commodities are likely to go up. Yet, according to our estimates, this will not exert pressure on the prices of processed food, but will only ease the disinflationary effect of the costs of raw materials currently trending low. As of October, one-year ahead inflation expectations of the financial sector have been running within the bounds of the target tolerance band, whereby the impact of this factor changed from inflationary to an almost neutral one. Taking all of the above into account, we expect year-on-year inflation in the on-going quarter to fall back within the bounds of the target tolerance band and continue to move within this range. Last yeard5s low base will gradually drive inflation up over the course of this year. On average, however, it should stand at around 4.0% annually, which corresponds to the inflation target of the National Bank of Serbia. The risks to the projection pertain mostly to movements in the prices of primary agricultural commodities and developments in the international environment, as well as, to a degree, to fiscal developments at home. * * * Having analysed the current and expected macroeconomic movements, the Executive Board of the National Bank of Serbia decided at its last meeting to maintain the key policy rate at 9.5%. Assuming that fiscal consolidation is implemented as planned, monetary policy easing in the period ahead will depend in particular on the strength of potential adverse effects of the Fedd5s QE tapering programme on the foreign exchange rate of the dinar and the countryd5s risk premium. I must reiterate that it is the emerging countries characterised by pronounced external imbalances that have shown to be the most sensitive to the Fedd5s cuts in asset purchases. In this regard, Serbia has made significant progress d0 the current account deficit in 2013 was halved relative to 2012 and equalled EUR 1.6 bln or 5.0% of GDP. We expect the deficit to remain broadly unchanged this year. However, although Serbiad5s external imbalances have lessened, the need for external sources of funding has persisted. Aware of the importance of sustainable public finances for the countryd5s macroeconomic stability, especially in light of the unstable international financial market, the National Bank of Serbia strongly endorses the Governmentd5s determination to implement fiscal consolidation measures and structural reforms. Consistent implementation of these measures would boost the domestic economyd5s resilience to external shocks, while a closed arrangement with the International Monetary Fund would help instil investors with a positive image of Serbia as an investment target.

Title: Speech at the Presentation of the August 2014 Inflation Report
text: NATIONAL BANK OF SERBIA Speech at the presentation of the Inflation Report d0 August 2014 Branko Hini., General Manager of the Directorate for Economic Research and Statistics Belgrade, 13 August 2014 Ladies and gentlemen, esteemed members of the press and fellow economists, Right after the presentation of the May Inflation Report, Serbia was hit by unprecedented floods. The effect of these floods on economic activity and foreign trade is negative, while the effect on inflation is negligible. That is to say that the floods exerted no major effect on food prices in an environment of low demand and a significant fall in international prices of primary agricultural commodities since mid-May. Year-on-year inflation continued to move below the lower bound of the target tolerance band over the past three months, measuring 2.1% in July. Based on our central projection, year-on-year inflation will return within the target tolerance band (4b11.5%) in the fourth quarter and stay therein until the end of the projection horizon. Unlike prices, production was affected by the flooding, especially in the sectors of energy, mining and agriculture. The inability to restore damaged production capacities within a short period of time is one of the reasons for the downward revision of our GDP growth projections for 2014 and 2015. Another reason is the need for stronger fiscal consolidation than anticipated earlier. As a result, GDP is projected to contract by 0.5% in 2014 and to stagnate in 2015. * * * In the period under review, the international environment was marked by the continuing geopolitical tensions. Potential tightening of these tensions, notably those relating to the crisis in Ukraine, could generate multiple negative effects at both global and local level. At global level, the intensification of geopolitical tensions could affect prices in international commodity markets and capital and energy flows, while the potential negative effects on the domestic economy range from reduced export opportunities to a rise in the country risk premium and a decrease in capital inflows. The euro area recovery proceeded in the second quarter and the blocd5s growth prospects for this and the next year have been slightly revised d0 hence, the euro area economy is expected to grow 1.1% in 2014 and 1.6% in 2015. But, the risk of further escalation of tensions in Ukraine continues to overshadow the nascent economic recovery of the euro area. Another hovering risk is the risk of deflation, which prompted the ECB to increase the degree of its monetary accommodation in June, by introducing, inter alia, for the first time ever a negative interest rate on deposit facilities. The ECB officials reiterated their readiness to use unconventional tools in the coming period should the circumstances warrant so. By contrast to the ECB, the Fed decided in its June and July meetings to proceed with the tapering of its quantitative easing programme. It is also expected that the Fed will raise its interest rate sometime next year. The dinar was under appreciation pressures for most of the second quarter, as a result of the falling country risk premium and increased non-resident investment in government securities. In addition to global factors, the fall in the country risk premium was aided by the announcement of additional fiscal consolidation measures. Thus, in the first ten days of June, EMBI for Serbia fell to 220 bp, a level last recorded in November 2007. In July, however, depreciation pressures emerged on the back of mounting geopolitical tensions, but also unfavourable news regarding the pace and scope of fiscal consolidation in the period ahead. To ease excessive short-term volatility of the exchange rate, the National Bank of Serbia intervened in the interbank foreign exchange market both on the sale and purchase side. It purchased EUR 170.0 million in the second quarter and net sold EUR 30.0 million in July. * * * Based on our estimates, GDP contracted in the second quarter by 1.1% s-a because of the damage caused by floods. On the expenditure side, a negative contribution is expected from net exports, given that energy imports increased and exports of manufacturing industry declined. As noted already, GDP growth projections for 2014 and 2015 have been revised down relative to the May Inflation Report due to the flooding effect and the announced sharper fiscal consolidation than anticipated earlier. GDP will fall by 0.5% in 2014 amid a downturn in agricultural production and dented activity in the sectors of mining and energy. The contribution of construction industry, on the other hand, should be positive owing to the reconstruction of destroyed and damaged facilities. We expect that positive impulses to the economy will also come from the recently launched programme of subsidised lending to the corporate sector. On the expenditure side, the contribution of net exports to GDP will remain positive this year, albeit smaller than previously estimated because of the expected higher imports of energy, construction materials and equipment, on the one hand, and lower exports of manufacturing industry, on the other. At the same time, the efforts to restore flood damage should have a positive impact on investments. As stated in the previous projection, due to the expected fiscal consolidation measures, the contribution of household and government consumption to GDP will remain negative both this and the next year. However, as additional fiscal consolidation measures have been announced, their negative contribution to GDP growth in 2015 will be higher than anticipated in the previous projection and will neutralise the expected positive contribution of net exports and investments. Growth in net exports next year is likely to be bolstered by further recovery in the euro area, whereas a rise in investments will be propped up by flood damage restoration efforts and Serbiad5s further progress in the European integration process. The methodology of balance of payments statistics has been changed since the May Inflation Report. As a consequence, the current account deficit was revised up, as well as foreign direct investments in the previous period. In 2013, the current account deficit reached 5.0% according to the earlier, and 6.5% of GDP according to the new methodology. However, though floods affected the foreign trade balance adversely, we expect that external imbalances will continue to narrow this year again. We estimate that the current account deficit in 2014, under the new methodology, will equal 5.9% of GDP. Further growth in exports is likely to be led by external demand, i.e. the recovery of our main foreign trade partners, while a decline in domestic demand in an environment of fiscal consolidation is likely to slow down the growth in imports. * * * Inflationary pressures stayed low in the second quarter. Consumer price growth of 0.8% was due primarily to the seasonal hike in prices of unprocessed food and travel arrangements. Persistently low inflationary pressures in the last and this year were supported by diminished cost-push pressures, notably in food production, dented domestic demand, falling inflation expectations and relative stability of the exchange rate. The fact that disinflationary pressures are of more durable character is indicated also by low core inflation, which has moved within the target tolerance band since October last year, reaching 2.6% year-on-year in July. For the sake of reminder, core inflation is the measure of change in consumer prices excluding prices of food, energy, cigarettes and alcohol. It represents the inflation component which is under the strongest impact of monetary policy measures. According to our estimates, year-on-year inflation will move below the lower bound of the target tolerance band in the third quarter. In the fourth quarter, it is likely to return within the target tolerance band and remain there until the end of the projection horizon. The movement of inflation below the lower bound of the target tolerance band as of March was due primarily to a higher than expected fall in unprocessed food prices. However, we estimate that the disinflationary impact of food prices will grow increasingly weaker, leading to inflationd5s return within the target band by the close of this year.
